speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it desirable to point out immediately the unfairness of the government having left consideration of this most important measure until the very end of the session. That fact of itself, it seems to me, is prima facie evi-
5236	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
denee of a desire on the part of the administration to exercise its power as a majority to press through this bill under circumstances which are most unfair to the minority in the house. I would point out that the government has known from the time it came into office that at this session a redistribution bill would have to be introduced. In the speech from the throne delivered on October 6 of last year an announcement was made by the administration that a redistribution measure would be brought in during the session. The bill was introduced on October 13, and was given first reading on that day. Second reading took place on November 25, at which time the bill was referred to a joint committee of the house for purposes of consideration, and if possible, arriving at an agreement with respect to what may be described as the redistribution map. These essential preliminaries were simply for the purpose of quickly getting the measure to the stage where hon. members on both sides of the house and of all parties in the house might confer together with respect to the defining of the boundaries of the constituencies embraced in the redistribution map. At the time the bill was given second reading, as leader of the opposition I suggested it might be advisable for members of the redistribution committee to convene before we adjourned at that stage of the session. Hon. members will recall that the adjournment took place last fall in the month of November. I suggested that advantage be taken of the recess to discuss the map so that at an early stage after resuming the house might have an opportunity of considering the measure in a regular and orderly fashion and not in a hurried fashion. When we resumed on January 30 of this year, apparently the committee had had no meetings at all. As time went along and the committee had had no meetings and no progress whatever had been made, I asked the Prime Minister if it was the intention of the government not to proceed at this session with the redistribution bill, and the Prime Minister said that it was the government's intention to proceed. A little later on my hon. friend and colleague from Quebec East again asked the same question of the ministry, pointing out that the general committee had not been called together, that the Quebec members on the committee had not been called into conference, and that no opportunity had been given for the discussion of the measure. That was as late as March 23. On the following day the committee was called together for the first time.

From that time forward until just a week or two ago it was only on rare occasions that members of the committee were brought together. In fact, the impression became general throughout the house that hon. members opposite had determined not to proceed with the bill at this session. It now appears that evidently what has been in the mind of the administration all along has been to have its followers leave the matter until the very last moment, and then bring in a bill fashioned pretty much by the administration itself to be driven through the house in the dying hours of the session.
In that regard may I say there is an ominous parallel with what occurred on the last occasion gerrymandering of constituencies took place in this parliament. As hon. members well know the practice fifty years ago, namely in 1882, -was for the government itself to frame and to bring in a map. Then, with the aid of its majority it pressed that map through the House of Commons. That practice was followed again under a Conservative administration in 1892. On both occasions there were what have come to be known as odious gerrymanders. In 1892 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then leader of the apposition in this House of Commons, drew attention to v'hat was in the mind of the government with respect to the gerrymandering of that time. His words were these:
The very fact that this measure has been postponed and put off until, I may say, the dying hours of the session, is in itself sufficient to deserve the most severe censure of this house.
These words are to be found in Hansard of May 31, 1892. He stated further:
I protest against this system too long indulged in by this government, of delaying their most important legislation until the last days of the session when members are naturally anxious to get away to their own business.
I say there is an ominous parallel between what was said by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on that occasion and what we on this side of the house are compelled to say to-day. This government also has adopted the practice of waiting until the end of the session to bring in its most contentious measures. It has deferred until the very end the measure with respect to the salary of the chairman of the tariff board, the measure with respect to radio broadcasting, and the contentious measure concerning shipping, the debate in connection with which was concluded only a day or two ago. Now, after the order paper is cleared of everything else, and it is over seven and a half months since parliament assembled for

Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
the present session, it brings in for discussion the redistribution measure. I say it brings the measure in; as a matter of fact, speaking technically the report of the committee was made to the house on Wednesday last. At that time the bill which is now before us was presented. Realizing how little was the opportunity for full and complete discussion at this stage of the session I suggested at the time that an effort still be made to have the committee continue its negotiations with a view to finding out whether or not an impartial measure, one which would appeal to the sense of fair play in all quarters of the house might not be reached. That overture was accepted. A committee composed of some of the senior members of the house was appointed to review the situation as it had developed up to that time. The committee met on Thursday and again on Friday. But on Friday night the Prime Minister asked the house to proceed immediately with the bill, notwithstanding the fact that a call had gone out to the members of the committee to meet again that very evening. What I fail to understand is why that committee did not meet again. What was the purpose of indicating to members of the committee that they should come together on Friday night and possibly continue their discussion on Saturday, if all the while the intention was that the committee should not meet at all?
May I point out that the Right Hon. Sir George Perley, a member of the committee, stated in this house on Thursday that he believed the committee was making headway with respect to the matter which had been referred to it. I quote his words as they appear at page 5198 of Hansard:
Sir George Perley: Mr. Speaker, some of us who have been discussing the difficulties in regard to redistribution have made some progress to-day, and we would like to have to-morrow morning to meet and go further into these matters in an effort to arrive at a conclusion.
"In an effort to arrive at a conclusion," showing that in the mind of the right hon. member for Argenteuil not only had considerable progress been made but that there was a prospect of the committee reaching a conclusion. The hon. member for Acadia, who was also on the committee, gave his impression to the house on Friday evening, and his impression was very similar to that of Sir George Perley, namely that the committee was getting together and that there was a prospect of reaching a conclusion which would be satisfactory to all parties concerned. I quote from Hansard, page 5232:
Mr. Robert Gardiner (Acadia):	I understand that the Prime Minister was just about
to move the adjournment of the house. Unfortunately, when this question was brought up I was waiting upstairs for the special committee of this house to meet, . . .
And later on the hon. member said:
... I consider that the committee had made splendid progress.
That was said after the hon. member had mentioned that there had been considerable discussion.
Unfortunately to-day the committee was able to meet only for a short time; because of other duties intervening we were unable to meet this afternoon. I am quite confident however that if the major parties of the house agree to restrain themselves and be calm on the subject we can arrive at a fairly satisfactory solution of the problem which will be beneficial to all concerned. I merely rose to say to the Prime Minister that I think he would be well advised to move the adjournment of the house over the week end for the purpose of having further parleys with a view to arriving at a reasonable conclusion.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that indicates very clearly that those who were nearest to the discussions, who had the clearest view of the redistribution map, were gradually coming together on a basis of fair play and equity, and that in their minds there was every possibility of a satisfactory conclusion being reached. Why then did they not continue this meeting on Friday evening, and why did they have no further meeting on Saturday? I am told that no sooner had the house adjourned than members of the committee were advised by hon. gentlemen opposite, or by one who was a member of the committee, that there was no use in the committee meeting, that it would come to the same thing in the end, that they would make no headway, and that the committee might just as well break off. I say, Mr. Chairman, that that feature, combined with the way in which the committee itself has been dragged along from month to month and from week to week, is an indication that the government has sought by a process of attrition to tire out and exhaust the patience and energies of the members of the house so that at this stage of the session it would be possible for them to press this measure through with the power which they have as a majority.
In this regard I wish to say another word, with respect to what the Prime Minister himself has said as to the function of a majority in parliament, in connection with this measure in particular. What the Prime Minister said a day or two ago in discussing this question is highly significant at this time. At page 5074 of Hansard will be found the words of my right hon. friend:
Having regard to the fact that this is 1933, however, I think there is great anxiety on the
5238	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
part of the house that the bill should be enacted, and if we are unable to do so by consent I suppose the only other way is to invoke the aid of what is sometimes called the brute majority,-
Now listen to the words which follow. The Prime Minister says, "sometimes called the brute majority." But he goes on to give his own views as to the way in which government is to be carried on. It is as follows:
-but which constitutes the means by which under democratic institutions we carry on government,-
Brute majority constitutes the means by which under democratic institutions we carry on government!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what is said.
That is what is said. I will read the passage again and allow the house itself to judge as to exactly what is said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
-if we are unable to do so by consent I suppose the only other way is to invoke the aid of what is sometimes called the brute majority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By the opposition.
Oh, oh.

The Prime
Minister now interjects "by the opposition." He did not say that when he was speaking. What he did then was to continue to give his own view.
You understood that.

-the aid of what is sometimes called the brute majority, but which constitutes the means by which under democratic institutions we carry on government, the history of which is very interesting but to refer to which would serve no good purpose.
In that statement the Prime Minister is I think, entirely wrong. Government may be carried on by majority rule, but it is majority arrived at as a result of discussion and argument, not by brute force in any shape or form. That expresses exactly the difference between us at the present time. The Prime Minister is putting his faith in what he says is sometimes called brute majority, and he is doing it because according to his own view as stated by himself, that is the way in which government is carried on under democratic institutions. May I point out that there are some institutions of government older even

than parliament in which in deciding matters which pertain essentially to justice, the rule of the majority does not prevail. The institution of the jury is a much older institution than parliament itself, and even our present day juries decide not by a majority but by common consensus of view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not in all cases.

In the most
important cases. And may I say with respect to a question like the redistribution of seats in the House of Commons, on which the whole basis of government itself rests, that this parliament is not merely exercising its function of legislating, it is exercising the function of the high court of parliament wherein it is expected to see that justice is done to all electors in the country, those who may not be in a position to represent their own views except by the members who happen to be representing them in particular constituencies at this time, as well as those who speak through their members. I submit that there is no higher trust imposed upon a House of Commons under our constitution than that of justly redistributing the constituencies. That trust is one which must be exercised not alone in the light of what is in the interest of the sitting member or the constituency he represents, but in a wholly or impartial and broadminded way in the light of what is most just and fair to the great body of the electorate.
What about 1924?

Ask York-Sunbury about
1924?

May I ask,
Mr. Chairman, if at the very beginning of this discussion we are to have interruptions and continual disorder from hon. gentlemen opposite as part of their brute majority method of procedure; or whether we are going to have-this discussion carried on as proceedings in parliament are supposed to be conducted? We have heard a good deal this session about the iron heel of ruthlessness and brute majority. If that is the way in which matters in parliament are to be decided I think the sooner hon. gentlemen opposite allow the public to have some say on procedure with respect to its affaire the better it will be.
I mentioned not long ago, when we were discussing the United Kingdom-Canada agreement, that I thought it would be desirable to let the public who were being adversely affected by its provisions have some say with.

Redistribution-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
respect to that measure. And what was the reply of my right hon. friend? It receives added significance in the light of what is taking place to-day. I said:
My right hon. friend says he will stand or fall by these agreements.
Mr. Bennett: Hear, hear.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I challenge him to go to the country upon this issue-
Mr. Bennett: Wait till we pass the representation bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

There you have the secret. And the Prime Minister says "hear, hear."
I just have this further to say, Mr. Chairman, that I think we might well reserve the decision as to the designation to be given to this measure until we see what it is to include. As it reads to-day it is:
This act may be cited as the Representation Act, 1932.
That, as it stands, will require amendment to 1933. I think if we are to proceed as hon. gentlemen opposite have indicated we may in the end have to change it to read, "The Brute Majority Representation Act, 1933." However, I shall reserve until later what I may have to say further on that.
I wish at the moment in conclusion to say this to the Prime Minister: The other evening he spoke of there having been threats of delay and the like. I wish to say to him at once that we are just as anxious to get away as hon. gentlemen opposite. We are making no threats of any kind beyond indicating the position which it will be necessary for us to take in opposing injustice and unfairness. If as this measure proceeds hon. gentlemen opposite show a disposition to do what is fair and just by way of amending the measure which they have presented to us they will find us quite prepared and ready to join with them in an effort to get this bill through with as little as possible in the way of discussion. But if hon. gentlemen opposite are going to say, "We have the majority; we are here and we are going to have this bill or nothing else," they must expect that those who stand for justice and fair play towards the people of this country will have something to say before the measure is put through.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as chairman of the special committee having charge of the preparation of the schedules for this bill I think it is appropriate that I should reply to the right hon. gentleman. Under the provisions
of the British North America Act it is the duty of a government, following the taking of a census, to proceed with the redistribution of the constituencies based on the population as disclosed by that census. It is not a duty that a government seeks or goes after voluntarily; it is a duty imposed upon a government by the constitution. In approaching the discharge of that duty let me assure the right hon. gentleman that this government has as high a conception of its responsibility and as keen an appreciation of the principles upon which a redistribution should be based as has been possessed by any other government in this Dominion.
The result of the census disclosed that a readjustment was necessary in the province of Nova Scotia, which must lose two seats, as well as in the province of New Brunswick, which must lose one seat. The province of British Columbia is entitled to two additional seats and the province of Alberta to one more seat. These are the only provinces in which the numbers must be varied as a result of this census. There are, however, changes to be made in the other provinces because of increases in population in certain areas, particularly in the cities, rendering a rearrangement necessary in those provinces also.
The course adopted was the course that was followed during the last two redistributions, the appointment of a special committee representative of all parties in this house. That committee was appointed in due course; it met and fully recognized the principles which had been laid down in this house by the leaders of all parties, namely that the unit of representation in the cities should be larger than the unit in the rural municipalities, and that there should be no greater disturbance of conditions than was absolutely necessary. That committee met, recognized and confirmed those principles, and it was unanimously agreed that it would be well to subdivide the committee into committees for each province and that these sub-committees should meet, discuss the situation, endeavour to arrive at an agreement and report to the general committee.
That course was followed; from time to time I saw that these sub-committees met, They had many meetings, but there were not many meetings of the general committee; no reason existed for many meetings of that committee, because until the sub-committees had exhausted their efforts or had arrived at a conclusion there was very little for the general committee to do. However, the general committee was called together in order to find out
5240	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
what progress had been made, and we were all delighted with the very substantial measure of agreement that had been reached. Let me say to my right hon. friend that the work of this special committee represents an agreement in regard to, I should say, between ninety and ninety^five per cent of the constituencies in the whole of this Dominion. There is no serious difficulty in the province of British Columbia, though a readjustment was necessary there. There is no serious difficulty in the province of Alberta. I will admit that with regard to Saskatchewan the differences seemed rather acute. There is an agreement in Manitoba. In Ontario a very substantial .measure of agreement was reached, and the same applies to Quebec.
No.

I said a substantial measure, and I know whereof I speak. There is no difficulty with regard to New Brunswick. As for Nova Scotia, we have come to at least a fifty per cent agreement, so when it is all added up there are very few seats as to which there is any difference between us. The special committee met and received the report of the sub-committees; we were assured that there had been a very substantial measure of agreement and that probably full agreement would be arrived at. But suddenly there developed in that committee a disposition on the part of some of our friends of the opposition to delay this measure. There became perfectly clear the desire that the measure should not pass this session.

Not at all;
quite the opposite.

At every meeting of the committee towards the last that desire became more apparent. I assured the committee from the beginning that it was the desire and the intention of the government that this bill should pass during this session.
At the last minute.

Not at the last
minute but at every meeting of the committee. I said it was in the public interest, and I believe it is in the public interest that this bill should be passed at this session.

May I interrupt my hon. friend for just a moment? I was asked by the Minister of Finance as to what was the wish of the opposition in this matter, and I told him distinctly that we

hoped that this bill would go through during this session, that we expected it to do so, and that has been our attitude throughout.
That is quite all right on the part of my right hon. friend, but he is not speaking for others.
I am speaking for the party.

As I say, the
committee met and endeavours were made to straighten out the small items as to which there were differences. We had some rather dramatic demonstrations in the committee. We had maps torn up; we had threats and invitations to mortal combat, and all that sort of thing-everything that was calculated to delay and to prevent the bringing about of an agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee any longer. I have placed before it certain facts relating to past legislation of which it can take cognizance as a preliminary to the discussion to take place on this important matter. With regard to brute force,
I may say that this House of Commons is not a zoo, but one of the houses of the Canadian parliament. If there is any force on this side of the chamber, it is the force of reason and the force of argument. I shall have other facts to lay before the committee as each constituency in the province of Quebec is called. The facts I have given do not refer to the subdivisions of the city of Quebec or the city of Montreal, they relate mostly to the Tural constituencies. I say to the government that we are here to defend the rights of the people. I am entitled to say that because I have presented petitions to this house signed by the heads of families. What I am doing now is simply expressing the wishes and beliefs of the people whom I have the honour to represent. I shall object to any elector being taken out of the actual limits or boundaries of the constituency of Temis-couata. I shall object whether he is a Conservative or a Liberal. Ever since I have had the honour of representing these people in the House of Commons I have been devoted to them and have tried to do my duty and I shall not let the government take one of them from me.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to
say a few words in reply to certain statements which have been made by the chairman of the redistribution committee. I am sure he will agree with me when I say that so far from attempting to postpone this matter until another session, on every possible occasion, both before the general committee and
Redistribution-Mr. Elliott

before the subcommittee dealing with the province of Ontario, I urged the advisability of bringing this matter, difficult although it is, to a conclusion at this session. There are many reasons why I think that redistribution at the present time is of more than ordinary importance. We are living in a very remarkable period in the history of this country. Throughout the different ridings, the people are being subjected to burdens and difficulties which they have not had to face at any other time, I hope that my attitude both before the general committee and the subcommittee was such as to indicate a very sincere desire to see brought into being a fair and just redistribution which would cause as little grief as possible to the people in the various ridings and upset conditions as they exist to-day to the least possible extent.
There is one point which I think should be stressed particularly at this time. We find that there has been an increase in urban population over what it was ten years ago. Before this committee enters further upon its deliberations, I should like to call the attention of each member to a matter which I think should be considered very carefully. Today we are living in a very remarkable period with a great deal of unemployment. That unemployment centres very largely in the cities and towns, and I do not believe that this is not an opportune time to increase the representation in the urban portions of this country at the expense of the rural portions. There is no question that to-day the rural ridings in many cases are much smaller than the urban ridings. But when you look at the vote that was polled you will see that very frequently a smaller vote was polled in the large urban ridings than in some of the small sized rural ridings. If I remember rightly the smallest vote polled in any riding at the last *election was polled in the Toronto South riding with a large population.
For the consideration of the committee in the deliberations which are to take place, I want again to renew the appeal which I have made repeatedly, that where there is a possibility of adjusting differences they be adjusted by not increasing at the present time urban representation at the expense of rural representation.
As to the manner in which the committee conducted its deliberations and as to whether the representatives of the opposition on that committee did everything in their power to have the redistribution pressed to a conclusion,
I really think that the chairman of that -special committee upon reconsideration.will be 
disposed to retract the statement he made that there was a disposition on the part of members of the opposition to delay or defer the business of that committee.

I want to be
perfectly fair to my hon. friend and to say that he did not urge the postponing of the consideration of the bill.. In fact, he was as keen as I w-as to have it passed this session. I do not charge him with anything of that kind, but I say that from other sources there did come objection.

I knew from the discussions we had had that the chairman would realize that he was not representing exactly what did take place in his remarks in regard to certain of the opposition members - at any rate. As a matter of fact, the impression I gained from attending that committee, and there was not a meeting of the general committee that I did not attend, was that the members of the opposition were all keen to have the matter forced to a conclusion this session. In a matter that involves as intimately as redistribution does the interests of the representatives of this house and of the people whom they represent, it is quite impossible for men chosen as the representatives in this house are chosen and as the members of the committee, representing cities and towns and rural communities were chosen, to agree or even to reach a substantial measure of agreement upon matters which so vitally affect the interests of the people they represent. With the Prime Minister in his seat and with many other members of the government in their seats I do renew the argument which I have made repeatedly that at a time like this, with as many in the cities and towns on relief as there are at the present time, and with that burden being borne to a substantial extent by the people in the rural communities, the adjustments so far as possible should be made without an increase of urban representation.
What does representation in the House of Commons mean after all? What is the effect of it? The effect is to give the people who are given increased representation a greater voice in the affairs of the country, and the effect of that is to advance the things that make more attractive life in the particular communities in which these people live. Surely, Mr. Chairman, we have had demonstrated to the people of this country in no uncertain way-I do not want to get into an appeal that looks like an appeal of one section of the country against another, because I think that is bad-that life in the

city and in these large centres is more attractive at the present time than it is in the rural centres. We are spending money to bring people back to the land. That is one of the great troubles that the country is facing to-day. Do you think you are going to bring about that result by increasing the representation of the cities and towns at a time like this when that increased representation means the elimination of certain ridings that have existed practically ever since confederation? That is a point which I think should be taken into very serious consideration by the committee in endeavouring to adjust differences where they exist, and where adjustments have to be made I want to urge again upon the committee that they be made if possible at the expense of the urban representation rather than at the expense of the rural representation.
At this stage I do not propose to enter into any long discussion over the effect of the redistribution on the particular province which I represent. I do want, however, to call the attention of the chairman of the special committee to the fact that even if only ten per cent of the ridings throughout this dominion are in actual dispute, just consider what that would mean in a fairly close election, for after all no one can forget the fact that at some time in the future an election will be held in these new ridings. There are 245 ridings in the Dominion of Canada. Assume that there are changes made in the redistribution which adversely affect the opposition in this house in only ten per cent of these ridings. That means 24 ridings, and very frequently that settles the question as to which party shall have its views enforced in this house.
I do not think at this stage I shall enter into the difficulties which have confronted the members of the committee in the province of Ontario. There are 82 seats in the province of Ontario, and it is not an easy matter to delimit boundaries by which certain constituencies which have existed ever since confederation shall be wiped out. I think there were 31 of those constituencies that were not touched. The committee put a great deal of time and work on the discussions concerning the province of Ontario. I regret very much that the differences have not been solved, but I am still hoping that they may be capable of some
measure of solution before the deliberations of this committee have concluded. I do not know that at the present time I could to any great advantage take up the time of the committee by further discussing these problems.

In the first instance we set out to take five seats from the rural communities. It was our intention to give three of those five seats to the urban communities and two to two rural seats which had largely increased in population. According to the recent census the population of West York in the province of Ontario is over 124,000. I suppose that redistribution carried out by a committee of the House of Commons will always be a very difficult task. I had the honour of being on the committee in 1924 and we found the task exceedingly difficult then, largely on account of the fact that the movement of population in Canada is from the rural parts to the urban centres, and that movement apparently is going to continue. We found the same difficulty on this occasion.
I am not going to cover the ground that has been covered by previous speakers, namely, that the committee was subdivided into subcommittees for the various provinces. Each provincial subcommittee of course proceeded to make the adjustments or -work upon them, assuming of course that if they could agree the main committee would have little or no discussion about it. In the committees it was the endeavour to hear all shades of political opinion and the fact that we nearly came to a settlement on the two western provinces is I think an indication that our work was fairly well done. It is a very difficult thing to satisfy everyone. Then in the somewhat small number of meetings of the general committee, naturally we became interested in the difficulties that were encountered as announced by the members of the smaller subcommittees dealing with those provinces in which they were not so fortunate in approaching agreement. I do not know, and I am not going to say that more meetings of the general committee would have been helpful, because I think after all disputes can be settled better by individuals chosen from the provinces working in the smaller committees. There is more hope of their getting together among themselves than if outside influences are brought to bear upon their deliberations. However, despite what our good friend the Minister of Public Works has said there was a persistent rumour going about the corridors of the house that the government were not extremely anixious about putting this bill through which I may say caused me some uneasiness at times. Indeed, I felt sometimes as though our work-a great deal of hard work-was going to result in having the whole thing put over. I for one, am extremely glad that it is to be settled. I believe that the
quicker matters of this kind are settled the better for all concerned, and I want to assure you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee, that I was not one of those who advocated delay. On the contrary, I felt that we should get this matter settled. I never heard any expression from any one in our group advocating delay, certainly no member of it suggested it to me.
After it became evident that the committee in at least three of the provinces could not entirely agree, it was suggested that a smaller committee selected from both sides of the house might see if it were possible to bring about an understanding between the members of the committees dealing with the various provinces. Under the chairmanship of the Right Hon. Sir George Perley we did make considerable progress. I was one of those who hoped that we should get every one of those difficulties adjusted. It looked as though in Ontario the matter could be straightened out. In Quebec we seemed to be making fair headway, but I do want to say that redistribution in Quebec is the most difficult thing I ever undertook to sit in upon and understand. I confess here and now that I do not understand it; the way in which constituencies in that province are laid out. It is to me more like a jig-saw puzzle than anything else. Personally I was prepared to view the matter from that standpoint and to give in to a greater extent than otherwise I should have felt constrained to do. Other hon. members may feel that they have been dealt with unfairly, and no doubt they can put up a good case. I am not here to express their point of view; so far as I am concerned the sub-committee to which I belonged came to an agreement, and I am prepared to stand by that agreement. I should have preferred some changes, and would like to see them made even yet if that can be done, but if those changes are not made I do not intend to raise any terrific row about the matter and detain the house at any great length. The government must take the responsibility for this measure, and if the schedules are within reason at all I am prepared to abide by them.
In 1924 we had to take the responsibility, and apparently that redistribution has been used as a yardstick on this occasion. Naturally when you see a constituency with 18,000 or 20,000 individuals constituting the electorate while a neighbouring constituency has three times that many it does not look like an equitable redistribution, but that has been the system pursued in the past and I doubt if we can change it very much on this occasion.
I just wish to add that so far as we were concerned, as members of the opposition, we were at the disposal of the committee on all occasions, ready and willing to try our best to bring about a reasonable settlement of the problems confronting us.

At
this stage of the discussion I should like to make just a few remarks. I had not _ intended to speak at this .point, but in view of the remarks of the Liberal member of the Ontario sub-committee with regard to urban and rural populations I feel that I should say a word. I believe my fellow members on the Quebec sub-committee will agree with me when I say that we really never discussed that point. \\ e had several suggestions with regard to Montreal; it was suggested that two, three and four additional seats should be given there. Almost immediately we dropped the suggestion of four additional seats. One evening I was in the room of my hon. friend from Laurier-Outremont together with several members from the province of Quebec when that matter was brought up, and I said that so far as we were concerned we would be quite satisfied if Montreal were given only two additional seats, but that if this was not felt to be fair we would also consider three additional seats. During the conversations I suggested that neither party should have to take the responsibility of deciding whether two or three additional seats should be given Montreal, and I proposed that we make a joint declaration to the newspapers as to any decision that might be arrived at. At all events, Mr. Chairman, with practically no controversy we agreed to recommend that three seats be added to Montreal, and we worked on that basis. Personally, as a rural member, I would have been agreeable to only two additional seats being given Montreal, but it was thought that this would not be fair. That is about all I wish to say at this stage, except to make a reference to my hon. friend from Temiscouata, who said he was not furnished with all the information he required. I believe that was only an oversight, and the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont has informed me that the hon. gentleman has been furnished with the information required.

At the outset I should like to say that the relations between the members of the Quebec sub-committee were most agreeable, but .1 should like to say just a word in order to show exactly how we proceeded. I do not want to betray any secrets; I do not think I am doing so, because it became a matter of public knowledge that room 272 was being used by the government members of the committee for their meetings. I want to say that I was extended every courtesy in that room, and that other hon. gentlemen on this side were likewise admitted, though perhaps not so often as I was, which is only natural. After we began meeting in this room we were shown a map

Redistribution-Mr. Merrier
which had been drawn, by some man who seemed to know his business. When this map was submitted to me, representing the minority on the Quebec sub-committee, I neither approved nor disapproved of it. I was told that this map represented the government proposals with regard to Quebec, and we discussed the matter on that basis, but later on changes were made. At one time the east end of the island of Montreal was to be joined to the county of L'Assomption, but we raised strenuous objections to that proposal, arguing that more than one-haif of the population of Montreal would be included in a rural district. That proposal was abandoned, and other changes were made following discussion. The counties of Beauharnois and Vaudreuil-Soulanges were to be joined according to the original map. This would have meant that the riding would be divided not only by the St. Lawrence river but also by a lake several miles wide, with no communication between the different parts. I understand there is a ferry that runs in the daytime, but at night, to get from Beauharnois to Vaudreuil-Sou-langes, one would have had to go to Montreal, a distance of fifty-five miles and return.
So far as representation in the city of Montreal is concerned, there are now three seats in that city and I have no excuses to offer in giving Montreal three seats. The increase in population in that city in the last ten years was twice as large as the population throughout Quebec, and on the map as first submitted the idea was to have two seats in the island of Montreal. Discussions took place and it was finally decided that there should be three new seats in the city of Montreal, one in the west end, one in the east end, which would be respectively Liberal and Conservative, and another seat in the west end comprising Rose-mount, which was supposed to be fair fighting ground for both parties, and that was agreed to. The gentlemen representing the government benches were up in my room, as suggested by the hon. member for Compton, and they thought that the plan we submitted was fair and equitable. And that, as far as I understand, is the plan which is to go through now.
I wish to go on record however, as a representative of the city of Montreal, as saying that we were entitled as a matter of fact to more than three seats; but seeing that three are given us we aTe going to take them, and I do not want to -accept any blame for that. I am representing the city of Montreal in this house and I took it upon myself to get as much as I could for that city.
Our committee discussed this matter very thoroughly. I do not think there are other committees that worked harder than we did. We worked far into the night on many occasions, and when it was thought that it might be advisable to get some of the wiser heads, or presumably wiser heads, to form a new committee, we, as representing the province of Quebec, were called in as technical experts or advisers, and through the courtesy of the members of this new committee we assisted at all their discussions. We were called upon to give our opinion, which we did, and I might say that the difficulties that existed when our committee was disbanded, or when it was superseded by this other committee, exist at the present moment.
Now this map of the province of Quebec, as has been said by the hon. member for West Edmonton, certainly resembles a jigsaw puzzle, and there is much concern in that province as to the result of this redistribution. On the part of the public and in the press there seems to be a pardonable curiosity as to the necessity of such wholesale readjustment. Nothing of the kind was done in previous redistributions for the reason that Quebec, with its fixed population, served as the unit of representation; and if acute criticism has not arisen at the present time, so far as redistribution in the province of Quebec is concerned, at least the curiosity of the public is excited and the question is being asked-What are the reasons for all these changes in Quebec?
The opinion of the members from this side of the house, so far as Quebec is concerned, was expressed in a letter to Mr. Dorion, the chairman of that committee, on April 27, when we suggested that the province of Quebec should be left as much as possible as it is. But there were certain changes that had to be made. It must be borne in mind that the counties of Yamaska, Beauharnois, Lapraiiie, Napierville and L'Islet were to disappear owing to their not having the required population, and in Bonaventure, Stanstead, Lake St. John, Sherbrooke, Shefford and Brome-Missis-quoi there were no changes whatever to be made.
I suggested therefore, in a letter to the chairman of our committee, that so far as the wiping out of certain counties was concerned, when that did occur the adjacent, contiguous counties should be put together as an integral whole and should not be divided up. I also suggested in that letter that owing to the increased population in Montreal the representation should take place on the principle, which we started off by laying down,
525U
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

that there should be increased representation in Montreal in the west and east, as I have indicated.
We discussed these matters as long as we could. We could not agree, and it is not my intention now to go into details. I understand that when the items in the schedules come up each of the members representing the counties affected will have his say in the matter. I certainly cannot understand however why only nine seats out of sixty-five in the province of Quebec have been left undisturbed.

At this stage of the proceedings I do not intend to discuss the individual troubles we have had with regard to the constituencies in Saskatchewan, but I wish to make a few general remarks more in reply to the remarks of the chairman of the committee.
At the outset, let me say that I hope that the remarks which I shall make at this time and later on in the discussion of this bill will be such that the Prime Minister may not again be called upon to refer to me as one of those who are arrogant and almost insolent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say any such
thing. If the hon. gentleman applies the remark to himself I certainly did not.
He referred to the members of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just look at the record.

Why were those words
used at all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because it represented the attitude of mind which hon. gentlemen were taking.
But they must apply to somebody.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Surely-to those who accept it. Let the hon. gentleman read what I said; I stand by it.

I have it here. At page
5076 of Hansard, on May 16, the Prime Minister, in reply to certain remarks made by the leader of the opposition, had this to say:
My right hon. friend opposite knows from long experience-and he has had a longer experience of the responsibilities of the head of a government than I have had-that there is a point always reached where you cannot expect men who belong to the majority to be told that they must subordinate entirely their views to the will of a sometimes arrogant and almost insolent minority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

But prior to that, the right hon. gentleman had said:
My advice to-day is, and I have inquired c-arefully, that certainly the map which our friends from Saskatchewan insist upon is practically their map or nothing.
And immediately after that he made the remarks which I have quoted with respect to the insolent minority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was discussing another
point; I was dealing with another phase of the matter. I said that there was always a point reached where majorities could not subordinate their views to a minority-a sometimes arrogant and insolent minority.

I am sorry if I misinterpreted the remarks of the right hon. gentleman. I have only this to say, that at no time during the discussion, in the committee or elsewhere, have I-certainly not knowingly -been insolent or arrogant. Now, apparently in the difficulties which the special committee of the house and the special committee of elder statesmen have met, all criticism is directed at the province of Saskatchewan. I have been told at various times that if we could come to an agreement the whole matter could be ironed out, that Saskatchewan seemed to be the stumbling block in the whole procedure. If that is true, the only thing I can say is that perhaps it is because Saskatchewan has been treated worse than any other province in the dominion in the matter of redistribution.
No.

Somebody says "no." As
an example, I cite the case of the hon. member for Melville. He is one of the oldest and the most respected members of this house. For over a quarter of a century he has been one of the leading figures in political life and agriculture in western Canada. It was decided deliberately to do away with the constituency of Melville and put the hon. member who now represents this constituency in with another hon. member of this house.

Will the hon. member
permit me to interrupt? I may say that since the hon. member for Melville's seat has been restored I have been asked from the other side of the house to move the boundary line back and eliminate it again.

The hon. member says that he has been asked to restore the original plan; that is not correct, Mr. Chairman.

Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

The hon. gentleman
must take my word for it; I made a statement and my hon. friend has no right to say that it is not correct.

The hon. member has no
right to say that I asked him to put it back.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He did not say that.

I did not say the hon.
member had asked.

You said you had been
asked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: From the other side.
I said I had been asked from the other side, and I ask the hon. member to accept my statement.

I accept the hon. member's
statement. At this stage I may say that I am speaking for the members from the province of Saskatchewan as their representative on the special committee dealing with redistribution. What was asked of the hon. member in connection with the restoration of his original plan was that instead of restoring the original lines, the town of Melville and certain other townships in that vicinity would be amalgamated with the proposed constituency of Touchwood, the new constituency to be called Melville. That is what was asked for from this side of the house. I am sure the Prime Minister will not disagree with what was suggested as the rearrangement, of another constituency in Saskatchewan. I refer to the constituency of Prince Albert, represented by the leader of the opposition. This constituency was so arranged that with a normal vote the leader of the opposition would be in the minority by seven or eight hundred or perhaps a few' more votes. But that was not the worst feature. The lines of the constituencies of Prince Albert and Melfort were so arranged that the boundary line would run through the farm of the present Minister of Agriculture. To my mind that shows a deliberate intention on the part of hon. members supporting the government from the province of Saskatchewan to force the leader of the opposition out of the constituency of Prince Albert and allow the Minister of Agriculture to run in that constituency.
It is difficult for anyone coming from the province of Saskatchewan to preserve the utmost decorum in the remarks he makes with regard to the redistribution of that province. I must say that all my dealings with the hon. member for Regina have been very decorous. We have been very agreeable and there has been nothing between us personally which
would lead to acrimonious feelings or difficulties of any kind. With regard to the chair-main of the committee, the Minister of Public Works, I must say that he always has been courteous to me. He has been most agreeable and ordinarily I would say he has been very fair. But the fact remains that whenever I went to discuss the question of the redistribution in Saskatchewan with the chairman of the committee or later on with members of the committee of elder statesmen,
I was always told that if I did not agree to the proposals made by the hon. member for Regina the bill would be forced through in spite of everything. It seems to me that that did not offer much chance for negotiation in connection with the redistribution of that province.

That is a strange kind
of conciliation.
Tory conciliation.

I should like to quote a
few of the remarks made by the Prime Minister when dealing with this matter on Friday last. At page 5230 of Hansard he said:
I have no desire that there should be placed upon the statute book an unfair redistribution, but I will not become a party to an unfair redistribution being put on the statute book by the will of the minority.
I have no objection to that statement and I heartily agree with it. I believe the Prime Minister was sincere in making those remarks. Later on he said:
There is no disagreement about New Brunswick; it loses one member. No _ county boundaries have been disturbed; nothing has been done except to drop one member from Saint John. In the province of Nova Scotia, because of the desire to maintain county boundaries as they exist at present, one of our own members finds himself living in a constituency that has fifty thousand people. He has made sacrifices in that direction which he says will legislate him out of the House of Commons. That does not look like gerrymandering. In the province of Prince Edward Island there has been no change at all.
If that procedure had been followed out in the province of Saskatchewan there would have been no difficulty.
And in Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It could not be followed out in Quebec.
Yes, it could.

There has been no change in the representation of Saskatchewan, and I have maintained from the start that all that
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

was necessary to be done in that province was to make minor adjustments to the various constituencies in order more nearly to equalize the population. But we find that not only has the matter of the equalization of population not been given particular regard but that various members now sitting in the house and representing certain constituencies have been forced out of their own into other constituencies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member a question? Is it not correct that during the past ten years there has been a . substantial move northward of the population?

I agree with that and I
will take it up later.

And a good deal of it
will go back south in the next few years.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

When the committee rose at one o clock I had been referring to the remarks made by the Prime Minister with regard to redistribution in the maritime provinces and had said that if that idea had been followed in Saskatchewan we could very easily have come to an agreement. I had referred to the constituencies of Melville and Prince Albert and had said that other members were being put out of their constituencies. The Prime Minister then interjected a question whether it was not a fact that the population was moving northward in the province of Saskatchewan and I agreed that it was. I am sure that the Prime Minister will not think me discourteous to him if later on in my remarks I refer to that matter.
I had referred to the members who had been put out of their constituencies or had been put into the same constituency with another member, I had referred to the constituency of Melville where the sitting member had been deprived of his seat in Melville and had been put in the same constituency with the member for Touchwood. The hon. member for Regina then interjected the remark that we had agreed later on to the restoration of his original plan. I stated at that time that we had agreed tentatively to the restoration of his original plan for the Touchwood seat provided that the town of Melville and certain other territory was included therein and that the constituency should be called Melville. But I want to say on that point, that while

we agreed to that, it was on the understanding that it would lead the way to further adjustments in various other seats of the province.
Under the redistribution as it appears in the schedule to the bill now before the house the hon. member for Yorkton is put in the same seat with the member for Touchwood. I submit that if the seat of Melville is restored to its original position as suggested by the committee at the present time, there is no necessity for the amalgamation of the two seats of Yorkton and Last Mountain. If the original Melville seat is restored it breaks down the argument that there is any necessity for the amalgamation of two seats in that part of the province.
Then there is the constituency of South Battleford which under the present plan is eliminated. A portion of it is put into the constituency of Kindersley, throwing the sitting member for South Battleford into the constituency with the present member for Kindersley. The constituency of North Battleford is in part thrown into the old constituency of South Battleford, and to my mind this is one of the most glaring instances of gerrymandering in the whole province. They take the seat of North Battleford and the old town of Battleford, and put them into the same constituency across the north branch of the Saskatchewan river. Certain portions of the old constituency of North Battleford are put into the new constituency which is to be called Battleford. Up to the present time the boundary line between the constituencies of North Battleford and South Battleford has been the Saskatchewan river. The citizens of Saskatchewan in that part of the province lying north of the Saskatchewan river have very little in common with the people on the south side of the river. The people of North Battleford and the people of the old town of Battleford have been at loggerheads ever since the new city of North Battleford was created, and I charge that this is a deliberate gerrymandering to throw the new seat of North Battleford in with the old town of Battleford.
Besides that, the seat of Redberry, as it is called in this bill, is a ridiculous sort of constituency no matter how you may look at it. It runs from the Saskatchewan river to the limit of population as at present, one hundred and fifty miles to the north. Besides that it runs to the west, north of the constituency of Battleford as it is now called, for some one hundred miles from the city of Battleford.

speechtext:
I would point out to the hon. member that we are on clause 1, the title of the bill.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but this discussion has been going on all morning.
