speechtext: I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend-
Previous speakers have introduced all the material that I am now using, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: They should not have done so.
I shall appeal to the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me just a moment, we are now on clause 1, which reads:
This act may be cited as The Representation Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: On that section, Mr. Chairman, discussion has taken place of the whole question of redistribution, commencing with the leader of the opposition and carried on continuously. I think there is no reason why the discussion should not now be allowed to continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is no objection, certainly. I apologize to the hon. member. I was simply trying to follow the rule.
I am sorry you interrupted me, Mr. Chairman, because now I am off the track.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry.

I was talking about the ridiculousness of the present proposal regarding the constituency of Rediberry. It makes it necessary for the returning officer, if he happens to live in the city of North Battle-ford, which I imagine he would, having to go around the north side of the constituency of Battleford for one hundred miles to the west. Then as far as the present population is concerned he goes one hundred and fifty miles north of the city. But that is not the end of the constituency. The constituency goes right to the northern part of the province. In the northern part of that constituency there lies a good quantity of arable land which at the present time is unsettled but which likely will be settled in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suppose it would have to be put in some seat.

Yes, and I have made a suggestion which I am sure the Prime Minister will agree is very much more reasonable than the one now proposed. I agree that the constituency of North Battleford has a very large population and should be; divided, but
when they throw in the constituency of South Battleford with it I say that the division is ridiculous and is clearly a case of gerrymand-ing. I say that the population of those two seats should be divided in an entirely different way. I say that the constituency of Battleford as now proposed should go north to the boundary of the province, just as does the constituency of Redberry. I say that North Battleford and South Battleford should not be put together in the same constituency. They should be divided.
Aside from those constituencies from which sitting members have been thrown out or thrown together into the same constituency, there is the case of my own constituency. I am a little diffident about speaking of it because at the very outset of the negotiations I had made the remark, and I still say, that they can do as they wish with my seat. But they have thrown me into an entirely new seat, and the thing I object to in connection with my seat is that they have thrown me into a seat at the expense of my leader. In a deliberate attempt, and I say it advisedly, to gerrymander the leader of the opposition out of his seat, they have put the best portion of his seat into the constituency in which I now live.	[DOT]
This morning mention was made of the fact that the constituency of Melville had been restored as a result of the agitation that had been carried on by the members from the province of Saskatchewan. It is true that that seat has been restored. It is also true, as I said a few moments ago, that we agreed to a certain restoration of the original plan of the hon. member for Regina, who was a member of the special committee on redistribution. I have also said that if, as bro_ posed in the bill, the seat of Melville was restored practically to its orginal size and boundaries, the argument for the amalgamation of any seats in that part of the province fell to the ground. I submitted to the hon. member for Regina and to the special committee of elder statesmen of the house, who were supposed to act as mediators between the members of the special committee and try to reach an agreement, a map showing that it was not necessary to amalgamate the two seats of Yorkton and Last Mountain as at present proposed.
In the restoration of the constituency of Melville we had a long, narrow seat lying to the north side of the Qu'Appelle river. Prior to the proposals made by the hon. member for Regina the constituency, of Qu'-Appelle was located south of the Qu'Appelle river. I had no objection to the location of that constituency except that I did say. it
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke.

constituted a very flagrant example of gerrymandering, because the southern boundary was not lying straight as it had been formerly, but was made to jog, running up and down for a distance of six miles, crossing and recrossing the railway, with no apparent reason whatever except to throw out Liberal votes and place Conservative votes in the Qu'-Appelle constituency. I said there was justification for the restoration of the Melville seat to the north side, because the same principle applies there. The Qu'Appelle river is a natural boundary, and it is only just that the constituency of Melville should extend along the natural boundary formed by the Qu'Appelle river and with the lines of railway in both Qu'Appelle and Melville constituencies, and running their entire length. I say however that there is no justification for putting in another long narrow seat, and I suggest my map was entirely justifiable. I am sure hon. members Tvho have studied the matter impartially must agree with my contention.
Suggestion has been made that my attitude and the attitude of other hon. members before the special committee was unreasonable, and that we had taken the position that we would accept our map or nothing. Every time I went to speak to the hon. member for Regina in connection with redistribution in the province of Saskatchewan he asked me if I would agree to the amalgamation of the two seats and the building in of a new one. I always said, "I cannot accept that." I did not see any necessity for it. Immediately the remark was made, "Well, what is the sense of us discussing any further? If we cannot agree to that we cannot get anywhere." I am not blaming the hon. member for Regina for the attitude he has taken. ,1 realize he was in a position where he had come down from Saskatchewan with a map he was told to put through, and he had no alternative.
I deny wholly that statement.
I accept the hon. member's denial and I will say that if he was not tied perhaps I should say that I was more or less tied not to accept that proposition.
That is a different thing.

But I still think I was
right in what I said. I tried to argue before the select committee of elder statesmen, the question as to the amalgamation of the two seats and the building in of a new one, but I did not have the opportunity. After the restoration of the Melville seat was proposed I went before that committee and tried to make the explanation I am now giving to the [Mr. Totzke.J
committee. Of course I was heard, but after speaking I was told that if I did not agree to the proposition suggested by the hon. member for Regina, wdth the possibility of very slight variations in boundaries here and there, the matter would be put through by force and in spite of me. That was the attitude I met all the way through negotiations from the chairman of the committee, from government members, and from the select committee of elder statesmen. Always I was more or less threatened with the suggestion that if I did not agree to the proposals made by the hon. member for Regina they would be put through anyway, and possibly would be worse than before. Finally, in an attempt to have some agreement before the matter was brought into the house or into this committee I prepared another map. I went to present it to the committee of elder statesmen, but found that only the two Liberal members on the committee and the leader of the group in the corner of the house were present. I laid the matter before Mr. Turnbull, and he said to me, "Is that the least you will take?" I said, "Substantially, yes." I did not have the opportunity of arguing the matter before the committee of elder statesmen, and I suggest I was placed in the position where anything I proposed was given no consideration until I accepted almost in entirety the proposals of the hon. member for Regina.
I wish to say only a few more words in outlining the position I took throughout the negotiations. On March 16 I received the first map from the hon. member for Regina. In the covering letter he made the following observations:
I gave considerable thought to your suggestion that the boundary lines should be moved to the north and found that in actual practice it was rather difficult to make a general application of that principle. In some cases the boundary line has been moved north on my proposed plan. In others, it has been extended south and in one instance, sufficiently to take in part of the territory south of the Saskatchewan river. I know this is contrary to the idea that natural boundaries should be recognized, but I can only point out that communication at the point in question is not difficult, and that there are either five or six ferries across the south Saskatchewan river in the area in question.
As I have spoken some time, I shall try to curtail my remarks. After receiving that letter I submitted to the hon. member for Regina a contra proposal in the form of a map. The covering letter, of which I wish to read a part, is dated March 27, and is as follows:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the twenty-fifth instant, and wish to submit the following in reply.

Redistribution-Mr. Totzke
You will recall that my first statement to yon in connection with the redistribution of the constituencies in Saskatchewan was, that as there was no change in number of the representation- from that province, the only excuse for making any alterations in the present boundaries of the various constituencies was that there should be a more equitable distribution of population among them. I also said that it was an- accepted principle, and in this I am supported by the statement of the chairman of the committee, the Hon. H. A. Stewart, that the unit of population should be considerably larger for urban districts than for rural.
In preparing the map which I submitted to you, this is the principle I have followed, although I admit that in one of the northern constituencies, namely Melfort the population was left a little above the unit. The other two seats, namely Prince Albert and North Battleford, while above the unit of population, each contain- a city and thus may be classed as urban constituencies. However, I submit that adjustments to the boundaries shown on my map could very readily be made to take care of any discrepancies in distribution of population without too radically disturbing the present boundaries.
I admit at once the comparatively large percentages of increase in population of the northern constituencies, but 1 submit that considerable of this increase has come from districts in the dried out areas in the southern part of the province, and the majority of these people, to my mind, will return to t-he-ir former homes when conditions return to normal, as I am sure- they will.
Perhaps I was not quite correct in that particular, because the census was taken in 1931, and quite a large number of the people who moved to the northern part of the province went up after it had been taken. However I still maintain a considerable number went up before, and a good many of them will return to their former homes. My letter continues:
There is also no doubt in my mind that certain areas in the northern constituencies, now occupied, cannot maintain their population and will of necessity have to be abandoned.
Then I included a list of the constituencies showing the percentage of increase in population in the last ten years. I do not think it necessary to burden the record with this information. Then my letter continues:
Now the increase in population for the province is 21-6 per cent, and this must be borne in mind when considering percentages of increase in the various constituencies. I shall draw to your attention only those districts in which there are marked discrepancies, and which do not bear out your claim in the matter of adjusting populations.
This letter refers to the first map submitted by the hon. member for Regina:
Touchwood had an increase in- population of only 7-2 per cent, and so perhaps should be a little larger than the unit for the province,
but as the unit works out at 43,861, and will be considerably smaller when allowance is made for larger urban units, it seems to me that the population in this district is far too large.
Maple Creek had an increase in population of 13-7 per cent, considerably below the average. and yet the population has been decreased under your plan.
Moose Jaw had an increase of only 0-02 per cent in population. This is an urban riding, but under your plan, the population has been decreased.
Qu'Appelle had an increase in population of
8[DOT] 8 per cent-very much below the average, and yet has a decrease in population under your plan.
Saskatoon had an increase in population of 48-9 per cent it is true, but this is an urban district and should have a considerably larger population than you give it. The new district, Hague, which you propose around Saskatoon, has only 1,077 less of a population.
Yorkton is an urban district, but the city of Yorkton has only about one-eighth the population of Saskatoon, and yet you make the district considerably larger in population than Saskatoon.
Now, if you will study my map. I think you will find that in the majority of the seats the population has been fairly placed, having regard for the unit of population which making allowance for the larger population allowed urban districts I would place at about 42,000.
Willow Bunch is a little high, and some of it could be put into Moose-Jaw, which is considerably too low.
Long Lake is a little low in population, and some could be added from Humboldt, which in turn could take more territory from Melfort. and possibly Prince Albert, which would more nearly equalize the population all around.
Rosetown also is below the unit, and here population could be taken from North Battle-ford to make adjustments in both seats.
The difficulty I found with the hon. member for Regina and the Saskatchewan members on that side of the house was that they claimed that if my proposals were followed the population which was taken from the other seats and put into these seats which they were trying to preserve would mean the defeat of their candidate. In reply I said I admitted that was substantially correct, that they could not go out of these districts into the area around them without getting a population which was more or less predominantly -Liberal; but I said at the time that I was not concerned particularly with the evenness of the population in the constituencies. I pointed out that in other provinces they had in certain constituencies a very small population and in others a very large population. I also said at that time that I was quite willing to go back to the present map of Saskatchewan and make alterations here and there which would more nearly equalize the discrepancies in the population, and that there
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

was no necessity for an entire new gerrymander of the province. To continue:
Now may I make some remarks regarding your plan in general. To my mind your map does not recognize the fact that the only changes required in our province are adjustments to more nearly equalize population. You are not, for example, consistent in the recognition of natural boundaries. For example, in Qu'Appelle you retain the Qu'Appelle valley as the northern boundary, yet in Kindersley, South Battleford, Long Lake and Hague, apparently no attention to natural boundaries has been given, yet the Qu'Appelle valley is more easily crossed than the Saskatchewan river. Then again, no apparent attention has been given to railway transportation in some districts, and, as everyone knows, in the wintertime and during wet spells this is the only way one can get around his constituency.
I must say that I cannot help but come to the conclusion that your proposal is a deliberate gerrymander, which is confirmed by the fact that a number of the sitting members are forced out of their present ridings into new ones.
With regard to your remarks as to the probable trend of population in the future, I am sure you will admit that there is little likelihood of any very large increase in our population during the next ten years, and hence our adjustments may fairly be made on present population.
Now, Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the proceedings, I do not know that I have anymore remarks to make. When we get into the schedules I intend to go over the districts one by one, and shows just the attitude I take in connection with each. But before I take my seat I wish to bring to the attention of the committee the one constituency which I think is the worst of all in Saskatchewan, that is the constituency of Long Lake. This constituency has been a little low in population, it is the only constituency in the whole province where a decrease of population has been shown during the last ten years. But it is bounded on all sides by natural boundaries, on the one side the Saskatchewan river and the Qu'Appelle river. On the east side is Last Mountain lake. As I said before, the Saskatchewan river can be crossed at various points by ferry, but on the west side of this particular constituency is this Last Mountain lake which is sixty or seventy miles long and there is no way of crossing except by rowboat or motorboat, there are no ferries on the lake. So if the member for the constituency lived on one side or the other of this lake he would have to go around the end of the lake to visit his constituents on the other side. And at Ihe same time any constituents who wished to visit their representative would have to do the same. At present it is all right, the representative lives in Regina and he can start out and go up the east side and down the
[Mr. Totzke.J
west side, but in the case of a member residing in the constituency this could not be done without a great deal of inconvenience and loss of time.
Then I also want to draw attention to the city of Regina whereby this proposal the hon. member for Regina suggests that only the city of Regina be in the constituency. It is true the population of Regina is large enough for a constituency, but I submit that the annexes and suburbs should not be thrown in with the rural area. There is what is known as North Regina, having about 800 population, I do not know the population of the other part. But I submit that in this case the suburbs of Regina should go with the city. The same applies to the city of Saskatoon, I say more of the surrounding parts should be taken into that constituency. The people of the city of Saskatoon are thrown into the new constituency of Hague under this proposal, it is very inconvenient. Having nothing in common with the people to the north of Saskatoon, they should be taken in with the city.
My time is up, and I will reserve my further remarks until the schedules reach the committee.

I
do not propose at the present moment to discuss the details of all the constituencies in the province of Saskatchewan, but merely to present to the house as well as I can the general problem with which the committee was confronted, the general plan which was adopted to deal with the problem, and the guiding of principles by which I was governed in coming to the conclusions to which I came. My hon. friend from Humboldt made one or two remarks which seemed to me to explain clearly the whole situation. At one stage of our negotiations he said he was not concerned very much with the populations, but, to use his own words, he was willing to go back to the old map of Saskatchewan and leave it as it was; there was no necessity for a new gerrymander.
A new one is good!
That was not my statement.
If my hon. friend will consult Hansard he will find that what I say is correct.
I wonder if the hon. gentleman will accept my word as I accepted his.

Not as to what you said in the house. I will leave it to Hansard.
In 1924 when the last redistribution took place in Saskatchewan, there was not a Conservative member from that province , in the house. There was only one Conservative mem-

Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull
ber from the northern part of the province here when the redistribution before that took place. But whatever took place in 1914 did not much affect the matter because the map of Saskatchewan was terribly altered in 1924. On that occasion the subcommittee for Saskatchewan consisted of the hon, member for Melville, who was then representing the city of Regina, and Mr. J. Fred Johnston, who then represented the constituency of Last Mountain, At that time this terrible natural boundary of Last Mountain Lake, which should be observed very strictly to-day, was in the centre of the constituency of Last Mountain.
Not in 1924.

Until 1924. In that year it was necessary to provide for new seats in the province, and the error was made in building those seats. With regard to the area immediately south of the South Saskatchewan and Qu'Appelle rivers, which includes eight of the present seats, there has been no great difference between myself and the hon. member for Humboldt; in fact our agreement has been so close that the press reporters attending the committee meetings have said there is no difference between us on that point. With regard to this boundary line of Qu'Appelle, to which my hon. friend referred a few moments ago, and which is in this southern portion, all I can say is that I understand that the boundary line is satisfactory to the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who represent the adjoining constituencies, and I see no very great reason why we should waste the time of the house in trying to disturb it.
That has nothing to do with it.

Taking the six seats immediately. north of the Qu'Appelle and South Saskatchewan rivers, which include Yorkton; Melville, Last Mountain, Long Lake, Rose-town and Kindersley, these seats presented an entirely new and difficult problem. In the first place, prior to the 1924 redistribution that territory was largely included in the three constituencies of Saltcoats, Last Mountain and Kindersley; it is true that the larger portion of the constituency of Yorkton was not in that area. By this arrangement made between the Liberal member for Regina and the Progressive member for Long Lake, of the new seats to be built into Saskatchewan three were built into that area, and the result of the 1925 election there should be observed after this-well, I should not call it an old gerrymander because I have not used that term, but in contrast with the new gerry-53719-332
mander we will call it a redistribution. As a result of what took place there the constituencies of Yorkton and Melville returned Liberal members, and remember that Melville was the constituency built in there by the then hon. member for Regina, who immediately forsook Regina and went to the new constituency, where he was returned in 1925 with a majority of over three thousand and in 1906 with a majority of over four thousand. The hon. member for Last Mountain was also elected by majorities greater than 1,500, while the new constituencies of Long Lake, Rosetown and Kindersley returned Progressive members to the house, this being practically the only area from which Progressive members were returned. Qu'Appelle and Mackenzie were the other two seats. With further reference to the redistribution of 1924, it will be recalled that in the parliament of 1921 there was only one Liberal member from the province of Saskatchewan. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition says that the results of the following elections proved their fairness or unfairness in that redistribution. In the first election after 1921 there were fifteen Liberals returned to the house instead of one.
You lacked $750,000 in that election.

When we come to discuss that we will discuss how much you got out of the Jacques Cartier cheque and how much you got out of the cheque from the Department of Public Works in Saskatchewan, to which the hon. member referred in this house the other day, and which he tried to make out was a cheque of the Saskatchewan relief commission.
I rise to a question of privilege. As the records of the province of Saskatchewan show-
Order.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I object to the statement made by the hon. member for Regina. He lives close to the seat of the provincial government in Saskatchewan, and the statement I made on the floor of this house can be verified by the papers which have been tabled.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must state his question of privilege.

The question of privilege is that the hon. member has accused me of receiving a bribe from some source,

Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull

which is absolutely untrue. Must I submit to that sort of thing? The hon. member for Regina knows that all the papers which have been tabled in the legislature prove the truth of what I stated the other day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member rises to a question of privilege, and I should like him to state it.
It was a most vicious attack.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want to understand the privilege the hon. member claims, and I should like him to say which words he wants withdrawn. I cannot listen to a speech on these matters.

Will you allow me to tell you? I thought you were listening. When the Minister of Labour was putting through his estimates having to do with unemployment I stated in this house that a certain member of parliament who now sits in the House of Commons received a cheque, diagonally across which was marked "Relief No. 1." I was that member of parliament, and I stated to the house the conditions under which I received that cheque. Then I directed a question to the minister as to how much of the money spent for unemployment relief in the province of Saskatchewan had been used for like purposes. This money was paid to me through the relief commission in lieu of land which they expropriated for road purposes, but now I am accused by the hon. member for Regina of receiving moneys to which I was not entitled.
I never said that.

Now I demand that the hon. member, who knows as well as anyone
does the facts in the case, retract the statement he has made, because he knows it is untrue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In all fairness I must hear the hon. member for Regina.
If I had said that the hon. member for South Battleford had received-
You did say it.
Sit down.
I will not sit down.

If I had said that the hon. member for South Battleford'had received a cheque to which he was not entitled I would withdraw that statement unhesitatingly, and if the hon. member is under the impression that I did make that remark I here and now relieve him of that misunderstanding. I do 
not think I ever made that statement, and I believe Hansard will bear me out. In any event I do not know of any cheque the hon. member ever received to which he was not entitled. What I did say was that he had received a cheque from the department of highways in Saskatchewan, which was marked "Relief No. 1" and which he then led the house to believe had been issued by the Saskatchewan relief commission for the purchase of land instead of for relief. The hon. member now says-[DOT]
Mr. Chairman-
Sit down.
No, I will not. I rise to a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Regina has the floor, and I think in all fairness he must be allowed to state his position. Then the hon. member for South Battleford may reply.

A few moments ago the hon. member said he got the cheque through the Saskatchewan relief commission. That cheque was for the purchase of soil, which was taken off his land to make a fill in a relief highway passing his farm. He was absolutely entitled to that cheque.
Then why bring it up?

Why bring up the
$750,000, which has nothing to do with this matter.
I was entitled to this money.
It was taken to cover another excavation.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell me what words he wants the hon. member to withdraw or retract?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member
knows he must accept the word of a colleague.

I have no recollection
of having said at any time that the hon. gentleman got it from some source other than that from which he himself said he had got it.
Does the hon. gentleman accept my word as to where I got it?

If the hon. member
says he got it from the department of highways that will be correct; but no matter where he says he got it, I will accept his word if he will get up and say it. As I was saying before this irrelevant interruption came, the fairness of redistribution according to the leader of the opposition, must be tested by the results it brings; that is what he says. The right hon. gentleman argues that because we elected eight members in Saskatchewan in 1930 the redistribution in 1924 must have been fair. Well, if that is the case, may I ask what happened in 1925 and 1926 when we did not elect any? Where was the fairness of the redistribution then? However, I am not going to discuss that question at the moment except to make this observation; whether in error or otherwise, more seats were built into the country immediately north of the South Saskatchewan river than there should have been in 1924. If it was an error, well and good, and if it was intentional that does not make the position any better.
That was the first problem. I may remark incidentally that when these seats were made in 1924 as I have described, the population was then 18,000 below the unit of population, and that in a part of the country that was not growing. One of these seats has actually decreased in population since then, while all others have increased slightly, particularly at the eastern end; so that in 1931 those six seats were between 51,000 and 52,000 below the 1931 unit of population, which unit of population bad increased, between 1921 and 1931, from 36,283 to 44,186. It was obvious therefore that in this area there were too many seats-quite obvious.
In the northern part of the province another problem presented itself. There were three seats there, Melfort, Prince Albert and North Battleford, which were away above the unit of population-seats which had grown enormously in the ten years between one census and the next. The population of North Battleford, according to the 1931 census, was 53,708, or an increase of 55.8 per cent; the population of Prince Albert was 50,896, or an increase of 30 per cent in the ten yearn; and
the population of Melfort was 52,688, or an increase of over 71 per cent in the ten year period. There was the second problem, that across the northern part of the province were three seats much too large, and in an area which was rapidly growing. There were six seats in the centre, much too small, in an area which was not growing rapidly, if at all, and there were three seats in the northern part of the province which, as I say, were much too large and in an area rapidly growing. This is the area which the hon. member for Humboldt says will fill up with settlers in the next ten years, and from which the hon. member for North Battleford tells us settlers will be leaving in a year or two.

I will attend to you
when I am speaking.

I think the hon. member
for Regina misunderstood me. What I said was that the North Battleford area contained a good deal of arable land which would lend itself to settlement. I did not say however that there would be settlers there.

If my hon. friend is
correct, the hon. gentleman from North Battleford is running true to form.
Like my hon. friend.

The hon. member for
Humboldt says that there is considerable arable land in that area. Now, having faced that situation, I conceived the idea that the proper way to remedy the error was to remedy it at the place it occurred, and accordingly I was of the opinion that, too many seats having been allotted in this area in the first place, and that the area having been represented by one member too many in the last ten years in comparison with the rest of the province, the right thing to do was to restore it to its proper representation, which could be done only by combining two or more seats so as to reduce the number.
The northern end of the province presented the exact converse of that situation. It was going to be too large for three seats, and I thought it would be better to make an extra seat where an increase in population had taken place. Another idea I had in mind in laying out the boundaries was that, the northern seats being placed where, in my opinion at any rate, growth of population would be most likely, and having some regard to the trend of population except in that area I have indicated, it was fair that the northern seat should start below the unit of population. That is not a new principle. My hon. friends, in making the 1924 redistribution, recognized the principle themselves and started the seats
Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull

of North Battleford, Prince Albert and Mel-fort, 4,556 in population below the unit at that time. With their growth of population they increased 24,714 above the unit, or an average of over 8,000 each higher than the unit of population. I therefore adopted the same principle followed by my hon. friends in 1924 with respect to the northern seats, believing that they should be started off fairly well below the unit of the province.
Having decided this, I had reached the conclusion in my own mind that a seat had to be removed from the central portion of the province and a new seat built in the northern part, and my map was prepared on that basis. The fact that the southern part of the province is satisfactory is, I think, some evidence at least of the fairness of the map I drew in the southern part.
Will my hon. friend pardon me? The southern part is not satisfactory, but I said I was willing to come to some understanding if other matters could be adjusted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members may not interrupt without permission.

Well, if it was not
entirely satisfactory down to the last section or township or range, at least there was no great dispute about it; there was nothing that could be regarded as being in the nature of a deliberate gerrymander or frameup. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I may say that the expression deliberate gerrymander, apart from the fact that members are not allowed to impute motives, has been a stock phrase with my hon. friend from Humboldt. The first communication i' had from him with reference to the' first map I submitted as the basis of the negotiations that had so far been carried on wras that it was a deliberate gerrymander, and the hon. gentleman has used that phrase in all discussions since. As I told him then, and as I repeat now, such expressions do not add to "the comity of nations"; rather, they tend to prevent agreement. My hon. friend from Humboldt had his own ideas as to how these matters should be fixed up. As I understood him. he came here with somebody else's ideas which he intended to carry out. In any event, his idea was that the proper thing to do was to perpetuate the error, and in order to retain these seats, which should never have been there in the first place, it would have been necessary to move all the boundaries northward, discommoding all the seats north of them. We should have had to do that if we were going to perpetuate the error committed in 1924, and because I could

not agree that this was, the right thing to do there was, as he has said, a deadlock from the start. He would come into my office and ask, "Have you given up the idea of amalgamating these seats and moving them northward?" I would reply, "Certainly not", and we would then agree that there was no use discussing details until that general principle had been settled. If at any time in the course of the negotiations I had abandoned my plan and accepted the plan put forward by the opposition, we should probably have got together later on with respect to the details. But I could not see that I was bound to do this in order to be fair. I did not accuse my hon. friend of being unfair or of trying to bring about a deliberate gerrymander merely because he did not adopt my plan, and I had hoped that he would not suggest any such thing because I did not adopt his. Apart from the fact that we have differed on this general principle, however, I may join with him in saying that our negotiations personally have been kindly and cordial, and if we do not part in agreement at least we part friends so far as redistribution is concerned.
That covers the general problem and practically the whole dispute which has been in existence between my hon. friend and myself with regard to the province of Saskatchewan. I said that these should be amalgamated, my hon. friend said that they should not; I said that a new seat should be built into the northern part of the province, my hon. friend said it should not. From the first day we met until the day the bill was brought into the house there was no recession by my hon. friend from that position. At no time during the whole proceeding did he offer one single concession. This matter came up very early in the course of the proceedings and in order to make my position clear, the question of the seat of the hon. member for Melville having arisen and I having amalgamated it in such a manner that the seat of the hon. member for Melville was divided into two parts, as was Yorkton; this question having arisen and the proposal having been objected to by the hon. member for Humboldt and I being accused of trying to gerrymander the hon. member for Melville out of his seat, I put myself on record in a letter dated April 27, 1933, reading as follows:
Mr. A. F. Totzke, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Re: Redistribution Dear Mr. Totzke,-
I understand that the principal objection to the redistribution map prepared by me is that it involves the disappearance of Melville as a

Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull
separate seat, and thereby seriously affects Mr. Motherwell. I have no desire to do anything that would look like being unkind to Mr. Motherwell, or any other member on either side of the house.
If, therefore, you can find some way of preparing a map that will not be unfair, and will provide for the retention of Melville seat, I will be quite prepared to reconsider the situation.
That has always been my attitude, expressed both verbally and in writing to the hon. member for Humboldt. I may say that a map in compliance with that letter has never been submitted to me. My hon. friend says that when you come' to draw a map there should be no regard for politics or anything but the rights of population, and with that theory I agree absolutely. That was one of the reasons that led me to refuse the map prepared by the hon. member for Humboldt. Member after member from both sides of the house came into my office. I discussed this map with them and member after member told me they had never looked at the. vote to see whether the map they were proposing was good or bad. If that is so, my hon. friends who presented me with the map were singularly fortunate from a political point of view in where they placed their lines. The result of that map was apparent to anyone.
Some statements have been made with regard to attacks made by me on two former ministers, but there has been nothing of the kind. I have been adopting the principle laid down this morning in the house by the leader of the opposition. He said that a map should not be drawn in the interests of the sitting member or in the interests of constituents, it should be drawn in the interests of the electors of the whole dominion. If it was a crime to disturb the seat of one of these right hon. gentlemen so as to make his chances of election less sure than it was before, then what about the proposed map of the hon. member for Humboldt? According to that map, the present Minister of Agriculture would have been out of his seat entirely so far as the vote at the last election was concerned. If my hon. friends say that they never looked at the vote, I say again that they were singularly fortunate in having placed the lines where they did.
I do not think it is right to say that any map I put forward would have put the Minister of Agriculture out of his seat.

Another criticism which was made of the map was that the boundary line between Prince Albert and Melfort passed through the farm of the Minister of Agriculture and left it open to him to run in either constituency. I do not know where the danger to the leader of the opposition lies, but pera
haps there is some. In the map made in 1924 an area at the forks of the South-Saskatchewan and North Saskatchewan rivers, running twelve miles on the north bank of the North Saskatchewan river and twenty-four miles on the south bank of the South Saskatchewan river was interjected into the constituency of Melfort. The area in question was some six miles wide and included between the forks of the river. In order to get to the southern portion of his territory from the northern portion, the candidate for Melfort had to pass through the territory which had been interjected into his constituency. I eliminated that by drawing my line straight north and south past the forks of the river. That line happened to run through the farm of the hon. member for Melfort but that was not the factor, in the placing of the line. It may have been a coincidence, but that was all. Perhaps the hon. member who drew the map in 1924 did not look at the votes, -but again I say he was singularly fortunate in where he placed his lines. These things are coincidences when my hon. friends do them but when we do them, they are deliberate gerrymandering.
The hon. member for Humboldt says that if we had pursued the same course in Saskatchewan as was followed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick he would have been quite satisfied and there would have been no trouble at all. We dropped a Conservative member in Nova Scotia and we dropped one in New Brunswick and I suppose if we had dropped Conservative members all along the line we would have got agreement. My hon. friend criticizes because members are being put out of their constituencies, but I wonder if he knows how many members in the province of Ontario were put out of their constituencies in 1924? I wonder if he knows how many members are being dropped to-day through constituencies being joined? In deciding boundaries should we not do what the right hon. the leader of the opposition says should be done, not decide them With regard to the sitting members or with regard to the constituencies but with regard to the larger interests of the electors of the Dominion of Canada.
My hon. friend complains that South Battle-ford and North Battleford have been put together. I do not see any great crime in that. They were put together provincially by my hon. friend's friends in the province of Saskatchewan and they remained together provincially under my own friends in that province. After an experience of ten years they are evidently satisfied to stay together. Why should there be any crime in keeping together people who have lived in such friendly relations provincially during that period? My hon. friend proposes that South Battleford
Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull

should be continued northwards to the northern limits of the province. He has told us at great length of the hardships the returning officers are put to in reaching the northern parts of the province, and he referred to the great hardships to be faced by the candidates. Why duplicate that? If one returning officer has to go up to look after North Battleford, why send up another to look after South Battleford? If two or three candidates have to go up to the northern territory to cover one constituency, why send up two or three more to cover another? It seems to me that the smaller number of candidates that will have to traverse the northern section of the province by canoe or dogteam, the better it will be for everyone concerned. I cannot see any justification for extending the boundaries to the northern part of the province. I may be charged with being inconsistent because of the extensions made in the constituency of Mackenzie, but the northern portions of that constituency can be handled from The Pas. If the candidate for Melfort has to handle that territory he will have to go to The Pas as best he can to reach the same territory as the candidate for Mackenzie.
Proceeding to amalgamate some of the seats in the central area and having observed that the growth of population was greater in Rose-town and Kindersley than in the seats east of there, I decided that the amalgamation should take place in the eastern rather than in the western end of that area, and I did take the four seats of Long Lake, Last Mountain, Yorkton and Melville and draw a map so as to convert these four seats into three. To do that I extended Long Lake east of the Last Mountain lake where it had been in days gone by, and I divided what was left of the other three seats by a boundary line running north and south. That boundary line was satisfactory to at least one member involved. With regard to another member I never heard any complaint. With regard to the third member there was long and loud complaint till at last there was that dramatic scene, absolute stage play, in the committee room when my hon. friend from Melville with the assistance of the hon. member for South Battleford mutilated the map of the hon. member for Humboldt in that scene which was intended to be dramatic and was intended for the press. That is one of the troubles of democracy in a country like this. You cannot always do what you think is absolutely the right thing if the feelings of the public are to be worked up by a stage play of that kind. I am still of :he opinion that the boundary line as drawn north and south and having no regard to whoever lives there, is the right line, the proper boundary line to have made for that constitu-
ency. But my hon. friends opposite were vociferous through inspired messages to the press and through their speeches in the committee which were made for the press, that a great injustice was being done, and we had the same old cry, that this was the seat of an old, long established member of the house, and that sympathy cry was played to the utmost limit. So following that, on Monday the fifteenth, I addressed another letter to the hon. member for Humboldt which reads as follows:
Mr. A. F. Totzke, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Totzke,-
I am sorry that I cannot arrive at any conclusion other than that the six seats lying immediately north of the South Saskatchewan and Qu'Appelle rivers, in view of the fact that they are deficient in population by 55,000-
That should be 51,000 or 52,000:
-and in view of the further fact that they have grown very little in the last ten years, should be reduced in number by at least one.
In the last map I submitted to you, a certain area has been included in the two seats of Touchwood and Yorkton-Melville with the boundary line placed north and south. Although nearly all of the old provincial constituency of north Qu'Appelle, formerly represented in the provincial house by the Hon. Dr. Motherwell, was included in the seat in which his farm is situated, objection is taken that the change deprives Dr. Motherwell of a constituency. While I cannot see the force of that objection, as he is still living in a constituency which is familiar territory to him, I am, nevertheless, prepared to go a considerable distance and to sacrifice some of my own views in order to promote an agreeable compromise.
I am, therefore, suggesting that this territory be divided by an east and west line, instead of north and south. In order to get a fair balance of population, the east and west line might be described as follows:
"Beginning at the eastern boundary of the province and following the old boundary between Yorkton and Melville to a point six miles east of the old boundary between Yorkton and Last Mountain, then north six miles, then west along the township line to the boundary between Touchwood and Long Lake (as shown in my present map)
That would give Dr. Motherwell a territory well served by railways, convenient to get at, well known to himself, and would appear to me to be an ideal seat.
With regard to Prince Albert, I will be prepared to make the southern boundary of that seat approximately on the line suggested by you.
I hope that this suggestion will settle the whole matter, in so far as Mr. Vallance and others in the committee on Saturday declared that if a change were made that would leave Mr. Motherwell approximately his old seat, they would withdraw all opposition. In any event, I understand that your objections now are as follows:
1.	With regard to North Battleford, South Battleford and Kindersley.

2.	With regard to the fact that Last Mountain Lake is a natural barrier that has not been recognized.
3.	The combining of a large portion of Melville with a large portion of Yorkton; which objection will be removed if the proposition now submitted to you is agreeable.
In order to promote prorogation, I would be glad if you would agree with me in a definition of the matters still in dispute between us.
Prior to the writing of that letter the hon. member for Humboldt had been in my room, and we had discussed the situation in Prince Albert. We had discussed the southern boundary for that seat, and either I in his presence or he in my presence drew a line, or we drew it between us, which still remains on my map, as the line he thought would be fair to the leader of the opposition.

The hon. member does not want to be unfair. He will recollect that I also asked for the eastern boundary of Prince Albert to be restored the way it was, taking off the portion that was put in from Melville.

I will not contradict my hon. friend, but I do not recollect it, and the line is not on the map. In any event I made the offer that is contained in this letter, agreeing to place the southern boundary of Prince Albert on exactly the line that my hon. friend from Humboldt indicated. I had thought then that all the matters in dispute between us had been settled. Lest they might not be I asked my hon. friend. I outlined in the letter those things which might still be in dispute between us and asked him if he would agree with me in defining the points in dispute so that we would know where our settlement came. Later he called me or I called him, or at any rate we got into conversation on the phone, and I asked him if the proposition contained in my letter was agreeable to him, and he said, "No, it is all off." I think those were his exact words. He said that the hon. member for Prince Albert would not buy any concession for himself at the expense of anybody else in the house. A perusal of my letter will show that there were no concessions asked on behalf of anybody else. An offer was made, and it was hoped that it would be accepted-that it would narrow, if not entirely remove, the issues between us. In any event the written offer was refused, and having been refused I did not feel that I could very well change the map that I had with the lines that had been agreed upon. That is the situation as it stands to-day with respect to the constituency of Prince Albert. If my hon. friend wishes to see an example of a constituency at all
like what my hon. friend has referred1 to he should look at the constituency of Maple Creek on an old map of Saskatchewan. It is true that there the unit of population is smaller, but on the other hand Maple Creek is a constituency 'that covers a very great area and it is a very hard constituency to handle. It is a country with a comparatively sparse population, and in view of that I did not see that there was any particular harm in making the unit a little smaller than for other seats.

As one of those whose constituency has been eliminated in the new electoral map as presented in the schedules to this bill, I should like to say a few words. I am also one of those unfortunate individuals of whom the hon. member for Regina speaks who lives only two or three miles from the boundary of his constituency. May I point out to the hon. member for Regina that in the twenty-six years that I have lived on that same piece of land I have been moved around with every redistribution bill, so possibly I should not have any kick because I am being moved once more. The hon. member, if he goes back twenty-six years, will remember that the old constituency of Battleford took in all that portion of western Saskatchewan as far south as the Saskatchewan river. That was in 1907. Then after the next redistribution bill I was placed in the Rosetown constituency. With the next redistribution I was placed in Kindersley, and then again in South Battleford.
As regards the 1924 redistribution bill the hon. member for Regina has pointed out that the hon. member for Melville and the hon. member for Last Mountain were two of the members from Saskatchewan on that committee. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Humboldt, in spite of all the gerrymandering that was supposed to have taken place in 1924, and in spite of us, in 1930 it was possible to elect eight Conservative members and two Tory Progressives. True, as he has said, in 1925 we were able, under the redistribution of 1924, to elect seventeen members, and we were able to support the late government on that redistribution. I believe he will also agree however that it was not because of the redistribution that those results were made possible. At that time in the west there was an agitation against a certain political group which had been in existence since 1921, and on that ground and that ground alone the members who were elected in Sas-

katchewan in 1925 came to parliament in the session of 1926.
After the hon. member for Humboldt and the hon. member for Regina had been deliberating for a very considerable period they found themselves at a deadlock, and it was suggested from some source or by some individual that a new committee not officially appointed might be set up to arrive at a conclusion. The hon. member for Melville and myself were chosen by the Saskatchewan group to sit in on the newly elected committee along with the hon. member for Saskatoon and the hon. member for Moose Jaw. The hon. member for Melville and myself along with the hon. member for Humboldt in the office of the last named hon. member drew up a new map, and in it laid down certain principles which we thought we should follow in arriving at a conclusion. I shall be quite frank with the committee by stating that the first principle we admitted was that we would not disturb any sitting member from the province of Saskatchewan, irrespective of his place in the house. We thought if we could redistribute the population with as little disturbance as possible of the boundaries new set out, we would be doing well. The second principle we laid down was that we would take rural constituencies, namely those constituencies one hundred per cent rural but containing small villages and hamlets, and set the population at from 40,000' to 44,000, a figure which we considered fair. For those semi-urban constituencies, namely those containing small cities or large towns, such as Moose Jaw, Swift Current, Yorkton, Battle-ford, and the larger centres of population other than large cities, we set anything from 44,000 to 46,000. And for the twTo larger cities of Regina and Saskatoon we set the figure of from 50,000 to 56,000. With those points in mind we set to work and presented a map in the office of the hon. member for Melville upon which occasion two hon. members opposite were present. At that time we were told very distinctly that it was impossible for them to accept the map. There was no further argument, and the committee never met again.
In the meantime I met the hon. member for Regina, upon which occasion he pointed out to me that the map which we had submitted would eliminate four Conservative members now sitting behind the government. I hastened to assure him then as I do now that it was not our intention to do any such thing. As has been pointed out hy the two previous speakers, the constituencies throughout the centre of the province were lacking in population, while three of the northern

constituencies had too large populations. We attempted to redistribute by moving gradually south that excess population in the northern part of the province without creating any undue disturbance, or creating any new seats, in the northern part of the province.
If hon. members would look at the constituency of South Battleford they would find that that portion which is and was predominately Liberal has been moved from the constituency of South Battleford and placed in the constituency of Kindersley. May I tell you, Mr. Chairman, and this committee through you, that immediately after the last election the Conservative candidate made the statement that if the southern end of South Battleford, namely that portion in which I live, was eliminated from the riding the Tories could win. Therefore I was not at all surprised when, upon the presentation of the redistribution map, I found that South Battleford had been eliminated, and that the portion which had been predominately Liberal had been put into Kindersley constituency. In the original map there was another rather peculiar feature, namely, that the newly proposed seat of Kindersley went down across the South Saskatchewan river, thereby taking in a portion of the present Swift Current constituency. Upon going through the vote for the last election to find out just where that portion of Swift Current stood in that election I found to my amazement that there was about 800 of a majority of Liberal votes. But the next time I looked at the map I found that that portion of Swift Current had been eliminated. The hon. member for Kindersley agreed with me this morning that it was eliminated on his suggestion.
It was opposed also by your member on the committee.

I .believe the hon. member is correct, in the first instance. The reason he opposed it was that our first attitude was that natural boundaries should be maintained The hon. member is quite correct there. But it was not at his instance it was removed. It was removed because of representations made by the sitting member for Kindersley.
The hon. member for Regina has given the date of a certain meeting of the redistribution committee which the hon. member for Melville and myself attended, and at which we probably played a rather important part. He has accused the hon. member for Melville and myself of putting on some stage play, and suggests that it had all been rehearsed. I can state truthfully that no such arrange-

ment Was entered into between the hon. member for .Melville and myself. Undoubtedly the hon. member for Melville had well prepared that which he was going to say, and I think the very results would indicate that he had well in hand the matter which he had under discussion that day. I hasten to assure the hon. member for Regina, however, that it was not on any agreement between the hon. member for Melville and myself that the events he has described took place.
Quite naturally I discussed the 1924 distribution with the hon. member for Melville who at that time was the only Liberal member west of the great lakes. He represented the Liberal party in Saskatchewan during the 1924 redistribution. Despite what the hon. member for Regina has said, the hon. member for Melville took his map to the late Senator Willoughby who was then residing in the city of Moose Jaw and with only a few very minor changes the senator agreed that the map was very fair. Having in view the fact that the province of Saskatchewan is not entitled in 1933 to greater representation than it had in 1904, it seems to me that the situation is rather tragic. Our whole representations were on the ground that we had no increase in our number of representatives and that with very little trouble we could have redistributed the excess population throughout the existing twenty-one constituencies, without to any appreciable extent disturbing either the boundaries of or the members now representing those constituencies. That is all I wish to say at this point, but I shall reserve my rights to speak again at a later stage.

Mr. Chairman, I do not desire with the other members for Saskatchewan to . monopolize the whole time, but it does occur to me that Hansard would read more intelligibly if we made out initial statements consecutively. Let me at the outset assure my good friend the Minister of Public Works that I have left my cane and any desire to use it just now in my room, possibly to remain there until the next redistribution period comes around.
Too bad!

Unless it is required, you know. But I have no desire today to engage in a controversy with anybody with regard to this matter. I think the fact that I am well out of my teens possibly accounts for the fire going out of my blood a little and the heat out of my tongue, especially after the long six months we have been engaged here during this session. Whatever else comes, I am going to try to be moderate to-day.
At the outset may I say that as far as the constituency of Melville is concerned I am quite satisfied with its present boundaries as outlined in the bill before the house. Of course there is a very conspicuous protuberance from it just opposite the village of Lebret that might possibly be whittled off, but that can be attended to when we come around to it. I am willing to take it the way the government gives it nothwithstanding that protuberance if they object to the change.
After all I do not think this is a very satisfactory way to settle this knotty question. We have had it discussed over and over again already, and now we are going over it so many times more, and then again we are to go over it by provinces. Is there not some more excellent way of settling this difficult question? We are now well on into May, outdoors is delightful, the fields are a glorious sight, the resurrection of spring brings new life to vegetation, the trees are bursting into leaf and bloom, the birds are mating, and here we are indoors disputing over a matter that in my estimation should be delegated to some impartial body that has no interest in the elections: Especially does that apply in those provinces in which there is disagreement. As a matteT of fact in all previous redistributions during this century the various subcommittees were able to come together and agree, and putting it through the house was only a matter of form. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if it is due to the cantankerousness of the opposition that we cannot agree this time, or is it because we have a government that has brought down an arbitrary and most unfair arrangement of constituencies? I remember quite well the redistribution of Sir Robert Borden's government in 1912, I think it was; we never knew there was a redistribution going through, it was never mentioned during the fallowing election. The same is true with regard to the preceding one of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and as far as I know, there, never was any word regarding the matter during the election that followed the redistribution of 1924. We never heard of it in our province, everyone was satisfied. Surely the. desire for a scrap has been well worked out of us this year, without prolonging this session just for pure cussedness on the part of any of us.
No, Mr. Chairman, with all respect to others that is not the. reason. We believe that a very serious injustice is being done, not only in Saskatchewan but elsewhere, by the provisions of this bill, Some might think that as my own seat has been conceded-at least

Well, anyway, I feel so appreciative that I am willing to spread it all over the whole government and its followers. It is immaterial to me as long as I do justice to the situation by expressing myself thus.
I am not going into the controversial side of the redistribution situation; I am under orders not to be too boisterous or belligerent, nor too long. Something has been said in regard to the redistribution of 1924. I think if the hon. member for Regina knew the facts he would not have made such statements as that arrangements were made whereby this one and that and the other got such and such a majority, including myself. Why, Mr. 
Chairman, even this government could not have arranged things to get a seat in Saskatchewan at that time. The policy of the then leader of the Conservative party was such that if all the angels in heaven had come down into Saskatchewan they could not have elected a Conservative. Think of the policy of the Conservative party with regard to the Crowsnest pass and the tariff and the Hudson Bay railway at that time. That is why, regardless of redistribution, regardless of boundary lines, there was not a Conservative elected in that province. In fact for nineteen long years there was not a single federal Conservative elected in Saskatchewan. It has been stated who the members of the subcommittee of 1924 were. There were at that time six provinces of the dominion which had not a Conservative member. So we had some difficulty in trying to get proper representation on some of the committees. In the province of Saskatchewan there were, I think, fifteen Progressives and one Liberal, your humble servant being the lone Liberal pelican upon the housetop at that time. Well I could not go to work and make a Tory member just to go on the redistribution committee. So we did the next best thing; when the Progressives and the Liberals arrived at an agreement as to the map-I think we had five new seats to place, making twenty-one, and that added to the difficulty-when we had arranged the map as we thought reasonably and as it would commend itself to the major committee, I then, as intimated by the hon. member for South Battleford, was instructed by the major committee to take our map to the late Senator Willoughby. He was then, I think, the leader of the Conservative party in the upper house. He had also been for many years leader of the Conservative opposition in the Regina house. I knew the late Senator Willoughby very well and quite favourably.
I went to him with the map and said it did not seem quite right that they should not have a voice in its formation. The fates seemed to be unkind to the Tory party for a number of years, but I did not anticipate that it would always be so, and my anticipation has been proven correct. Therefore I said we would feel more comfortable if he would take our map and look it over. He asked if he could keep it and I said yes, that he might keep it three or four days in order to consult with whatever colleagues he chose. If I remember correctly I mentioned Senator Calder, but I am not sure; at all events I left it to the late Senator Willoughby to consult with whatever Conservative colleagues he had in Saskatchewan, and I am sure he had at least

two or three. At the expiration of the three or four days I went back to his office and asked if there were any particular changes he would like. He mentioned two, the first of which 'we the subcommittee had already considered and met his wishes. It was a trifling matter, and is not worth mentioning now. I asked what the other change was, and he said he would like six townships taken out of the riding of Qu'Appelle and attached to the riding of Wey-burn, immediately south. I suppose these six ridings merely happened to have strong Liberal majorities. I said to the Senator, "Well, if we concede this change it will be decidedly in your interest, because Weyburn does not really need it while Qu'Appelle will be very glad to get rid of those troublesome townships." In this redistribution bill the Conservatives still show that desire to get rid of that Liberal area, in Qu'Appelle and many other similar areas as well. The senator replied, "Well, you do not expect me to make a recommendation against my own side, do you?" I admitted that I did not, and then I asked if those were the only recommendations he desired to make with regard to the twenty-one ridings in Sakatchewan, if all he asked was that those six townships should be transferred from the south of one riding to the north of the other, and he said that was all. I told him that so far as I was concerned he could have that change made, and I stated that I would so report to the main committee. I conferred with Fred Johnston before reporting; when we presented that suggestion to the main committee they smiled a little at our simplicity. I said, "Will it not be worth that concession to be able to say that the map was referred to the only Conservative representatives we could find?" In those days they were as hard to discover as a needle in a haystack, and we took the only course we could. I suggested that it would be worth while to be able to say that after the map had been referred to some representative Conservatives the only changes they requested were fully complied with. From a political standpoint as well as from the point of view of being right it was worth many times the loss of the six townships, so we were not quite so simple minded as we appeared. It was fair and right, and after all is not the right and fair thing the proper thing to do even in politics? You may look simple at the time for doing it, but it will be like bread cast upon the waters; it will come back some time, perhaps in a few days rather than many.
I do not know whether or not hon. gentlemen opposite believe that story; I cannot say I do not care, because I do care. If we had some sort of tribunal, however, to which we
could refer these matters, when any responsible person made a statement such as I have just made we could easily call witnesses before that body. In my case I could wire for Fred Johnston and John Millar or any others who know the facts.
And Senator Willoughby?

I will not wait to ask my hon. friend to repeat what he said. We could get also the hon. member for Weyburn as he has some knowledge of the matter. These are some of the reasons why I dislike the thought of spending these beautiful spring days inside in unprofitable discussion of this controversial matter, but it is not our fault. An unjust and unfair redistribution of constituencies has been offered this house by the government; we do not like it, and we are going to show our opposition in all legitimate ways. I hope the discussion will continue to be legitimate and orderly, but if it is not the responsibility must be borne by the government.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I have covered what I had in mind when I made these few notes this afternoon. I feel like making an appeal to the Prime Minister; perhaps because my last appeal was successful I feel like making another. Why the haste? We started the last distribution in 1923, but it took two years. Rather than press it on some unwilling members in 1923 we deferred the decision until 1924. Was that not a better way than to scrap it out or threaten to put it through by closure? I said some pretty caustic things about the Prime Minister's experience in London at his first conference, and again with regard to the Ottawa conference. Now I want to say some nice things about his experience in Washington, where he conducted himself in a manner which made us all proud of him. Would it not be better for him to leave the shores of Canada with everything nice and peaceful on parliament hill than to have just finished a great big scrap over redistribution?
A bribe?

It is a justifiable bribe if it is a bribe at all. I am putting it as I think my hon. friend from Parkdale would put it in his own heart. Anyone who has been at one of these great conferences knows that the person who represents Canada or any other country must have a period of quiet, rest and study to prepare therefor, and if the Prime Minister would follow that course I am sure no man at the conference would acquit himself better from his viewpoint than the same right hon. gentleman. But if he goes there with his nerves all ruffled

How about blarney?

If hon. gentlemen
opposite want to know. my composition I will give it to them; it may account for some of my belligerency and indignation when I find myself put upon. Then a race - for the train; a race for the boat; a race for London, fire and brimstone breathing all across the way; and then you expect to soothe down the ruffled feelings of the nations of the world on the many knotty problems that will come up on that occasion before a thus harassed and hurried Canadian Prime Minister. I do not believe it is fair and I appeal to the Prime Minister as our Prime' Minister, as my Prime Minister-the best one I can get for the present, and so long as it is by the will of the people, whoever is Prime Minister, is my Prime Minister, no matter what side he is on.
I would acknowledge the same if the C.C. F.'ers were in power, though I rather hope that will not occur in my lifetime, But joking aside, I think that most of us. feel, that while we have been looking forward for nearly three years hoping for accomplishments, nothing worth while has really been done yet. First there was the, London, conference, then the Ottawa conference, then the Washington conference; and now we have been told, "Hurrah,.boys, the real thing is coming at the [Mr. Motherwell.)
London 'conference on June 12th." Well, if that is to be the climax, if it is to be a case of to be or not to be, then I say, let us not spoil the setting, the home leaving for the Prime Minister by dealing with this matter at this time. That would be my invocation, that would be my last word at this stage of the debate, and I have a sort of half belief that whatever the Prime Minister may do or say in response to my appeal he would like to do as I suggest himself. But the exigencies of the situation, the possibility of an election this fall, and the desire to reap any benefit that might accrue to the governing party by reason of this redistribution all urge him to have it over first and get it off his hands, so that the government will be free to go to the people at any time. I can quite understand that. But will not that advantage be largely lost, will it not be dissipated if he drives this unjust measure through the house? The Minister of Public Works said a bib-full during his short remarks when he intimated that there was such a thing as a brute minority. Yes, there is, if we choose to exercise it. Five men backed bv other speakers desirous of going the limit, and without any violence, could compel this government to 'abandon this bill before the conference if they wanted to.
