Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): As one of the members from western Canada affected by this notorious redistribution bill, I think I should say a few words in this house. The measure before us is described as "Bill 2, an Act to readjust the Representation in the House of Commons." The understanding implied by that title is that the readjustment of representation is to be brought about by a government having a fair majority in parliament and not by a government which will use in an unfair way the majority given to it by the people; not by a government anxious to make use of a brute majority in the national assembly. At the present moment we are not sure what the government is going to do; in other words, the government has not yet put its cards on the table to show how it will get the measure through the house. We shall see that by and by, but I hesitate to believe that the best thinking members on the other side of the chamber, the Prime Minister himself or any one of his cabinet members, will attempt to drive a measure of this kind through the House of Commons by means of the gag, by brute majority. I hesitate to believe that until I see it. However, if that attempt is made, the members from western Canada will explain in no uncertain terms their attitude towards any such endeavour.
May I now briefly review two or three points leading up to this measure. May I say .first of all that the work of redistribution in Canada is nothing new; it has taken place periodically from 1867, over sixty years ago. Under the British North America Act redistribution is necessary every ten years, and I think, it is worth while going back over past history to see how the work of redistribution has been effected from decade to decade. In 1872 there was a redistribution following confederation; there was another in 1882, and one again in 1892. During the period covered by those three redistributions the Conservatives were in power. We have been told-and I am not mistaken-at least it has been re-echoed by quite a number of Conservatives from the west, that this is their first chance, their glorious opportunity for a gerrymander. They have stated that they have not had an opportunity to carry out a redistribution to their taste for quite a long time and they therefore
must take advantage of the present occasion to do their best in order to improve their chances at the polls. There we have their viewpoint as explained by themselves, calculatingly, coldly, callously.
Well, in 1872 and 1882 right up to 1892 the party opposite was in power and had charge of three redistributions, and I would point out first of all that the redistribution of 1872 was put through the house, not upon the report of any joint committee but by a brute majority; it was driven through the house. The redistribution was effected in a similar way in 1882 and in 1892. When we come to 1903 we find the Liberals in power, and the redistribution in 1903 and that carried out in 1924 were the only two occasions when the Liberals effected a readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. Both these redistributions were as fair as possible. Since confederation, of seven redistributions, five have been made by Conservatives and only two by the Liberals; in other words, the Conservatives have had more than twice as many redistributions under their charge as the Liberals have put through the house.
All redistributions up until 1903 were carried out in about the same way, not by a report of a joint committee, not in a conciliatory manner, not by cooperation, but by using the majority in the House of Commons to drive partisan redistribution measures through the house. In 1903 a change took place. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a great Canadian, was at the helm of state. What did he do? He turned his back on work of that kind, he would not accept it. He arranged for a joint committee to take up the work and try to obtain a decent solution of the problem. Things were worked out in a fair and just way. In 1911, after the success of 1903, Sir Robert Borden, another eminent Canadian, was at the head of affairs and he followed the practice launched by Laurier in 1903. If I am not mistaken the present Prime Minister was a member of that redistribution committee, and if any hon. member of this committee ought to know what was done and what ought to be done now, it is the Prime Minister. I am just fair enough to believe that before this debate continues much longer the Prime Minister will rise to the occasion and take such action as will enable the committee which was dealing with this measure, or the last elderly committee which was dealing with it, to take up the matter anew and so iron out all difficulties that the work of redistribution will be done fairly and honourably.
The hon. member for Regina said that in 1924 there was not one Conservative from

The hon. member for Regina attempted to make out that he was following that plan, that there were too many seats made in central Saskatchewan in 1924 and that one would have to be eliminated. Let me tell the committee what he and the Conservative party have done in this bill as far as the federal riding of North Battleford is concerned. They have taken two-thirds or more of that riding which they figure consists

of Liberal votes and made a new riding with the addition of a few polls from across the North Saskatchewan river at the northern end of the Rosetown riding. Just fancy such a base partisan move! May I say that I live in the city of North Battleford. and the boundary of the new riding in which they have hived the 'Grits, the constituency of Redberry, is only about three and a half or four miles from the city of North Battleford. I live in that city, and I am not in my old riding because I figure my old riding is over two-thirds of the North Battleford riding which has been intentionally wiped out and given a new name, having had an addition made to it-as I have explained-from the south. Fancy any representative, or fair parliamentary committee submitting to an insulting proposition of that kind 1 I would imagine that the very look of the thing would be extremely obnoxious and antagonistic to any man with a fair mind. But up to the present time, although representations have been made, the hon. member has made no attempt to remedy that monstrosity. The riding of North Battleford as it now exists is simply a curved geographical monstrosity. It has been cut to pieces and a third of it joined to two-thirds of the Battleford riding to make what the hon. member for Regina considers a Conservative riding. That is deliberate gerrymandering. What could one call it if not that? It is interfering with the franchise rights of the people affected. There is nothing fair or just about it. There is not an elector that I know of who will say that that is a fair redistribution either as to the top or northern part of the Battleford riding or the gerrymandered parts of the North Battleford constituency. Outside of a few Tories in North Battleford from whom the hon. member for Regina had to hear-as the hon. member told me himself-before he could make any changes, no citizen will regard this redistribution as equitable and fair. He cannot deny that.
I do not think that is very fairly put.
I do not want to misquote the hon. member. I have a great respect for him except in some regards.
If my hon. friend will quote the rest of the conversation he will see that it is not what he said.

With certain reservations I have a wholesome respect for the hon. member, but I am afraid he is slipping, dangerously slipping. I fear he is going astray. I am afraid he is destroying his own reputation in the province. I am satisfied he is destroying his own reputation in the city of Regina. I am convinced he has done something here that will be tagged to him for the rest of his life. I only spoke to the hon. member once or twice about this measure. I deliberately kept away from him, I wanted him to have has own free will about it. But I had an idea what was going on all the time, and when I did speak to him about it he said, "I will consider the matter," but I do not think he has given the consideration promised. But he did say-yes he did-that he had to hear from North Battleford before he could do anything. He was expecting to hear from a small Tory clique who were bent on manipulating votes. These men were back of my hon. friend from Regina, these and other Conservatives from the province. These men were tied to the committee in Regina that, in the main, worked out this redistribution bill. There is no doubt about it that the map which my hon. friend submitted in the first place was wilfully concocted in Regina, and is the product of a Tory clique representative of every riding in Saskatchewan.
In the month of January, during the parliamentary recess, there was a meeting held in Saskatoon, and my hon. friend from Regina was at that meeting. I ask him now to deny it if he was not. Get up and deny it if you can.
That is no crime.
You cannot deny it.

Oh yes, it was. Let me go on. At that meeting in Saskatoon, the ground work was laid for the present gerrymandering in the province of Saskatchewan. There it was concocted and organized, and the hon. member for Regina was present and let it go on, and now he is trying to carry it out. Let me say, though, that if a few Tories in the city of North Battleford figure they can do what the hon. member for Regina and his government are trying to get away with in this bill, they have another think coming, and my hon. friend and the government will find out when it is too late what the electors of South Battleford and North Battleford think of what you are attempting to do in this bill.
May I say that North Battleford and South Battleford, as my hon. friend from Regina stated, are linked up electorally in a provincial way. We have had provineially a Liberal member representing the Battlefords and we have had a Conservative member representing the Battlefords, and I think I can truthfully say that the conclusion of both these members is that the tying up of the Battlefords is a mistake and should not be done, that they

ought to be separated electorally each with its own member, when the servicing of each riding could be better looked after. Not that I have any fault to find with the estimable people south of the river. I know a great number of them. I know every person in South Battleford just as well as I do the citizens in North Battleford, and my policy on the platform and in the press has always been-over a period of twenty years-to unite the two Battlefords-to bind them together commercially. But historically they were divided years ago and they remain divided by the north Saskatchewan river to a great extent to-day. My argument is that they ought to be left separate electorally. If the government is willing to make the fair adjustments that ought to be made, these two ridings do not need to be thrown together. A fair redistribution can be made by having the dividing line north and south.
The hon. member for Humboldt said that by pushing north the boundary line of the map which was delivered by my hon. friend to the Saskatchewan Liberals the problem could be solved. So it can, and it should be solved in this way if the government wants to do the right thing. Then North Battleford would be left in its right geographical setting. It is the largest centre north of the north Saskatchewan river between Saskatoon and Edmonton. That means something and if an outstanding fact it ought to be respected
That north country belongs to North Battleford. We have done our best to give it railroad and highway service, and I for one object to taking North Battleford out of its propeT electoral setting and putting it into a riding linked up with points southward and eastward, many of which are tributary to Saskatoon and other centres. The very fact that that was done indicates the motive. There could be no other motive than that of hiving the Grits in one riding and hiving the Tories in another, with the idea of gaining an extra seat in this house. If that is the intention of the hon. member and of the government I am afraid when they count the votes at the next election they will receive a surprise. I am convinced clean fair-minded people will oppose a policy of that kind; they will oppose any manipulation of ridings for the purpose of gaining votes, no matter what party does it. And they are right.
The placing of North Battleford city in a riding comprised of say one-third of the old riding of North Battleford and two-thirds of the old riding of South Battleford is admittedly a major grievance against this bill in the northwestern section of Saskatchewan. I

believe these changes have been made deliberately-not to put " The Battlefords " together but wholly because wholesale gerrymandering had been decided upon. May I say to the hon. member for Regina-and I see him pallidly looking at me-

But may I say to my hon. friend that a great many of the people who have come from the south to the north will return to the south-they are going now-once crop conditions and weather conditions prevail which will make it worth their while. They will return when they have a better opportunity to make a living in the southern part of the province than there has been in the last few years. The population in the northern part has grown considerably during the last ten years, but many of those who came from the south will go back. The population will be balanced better than it is to-day. Many in the north are on farms upon which they cannot make a living, and they will have to leave for other parts. Many of them are on relief at the present time, and that condition of affairs cannot continue. They are not to blame. I suggest that to base a redistribution on such changing conditions is not sound.
I am not going to say anything further at the present time. All I wanted to do was to give the house an idea of what has been done to the two ridings of North Battleford and South Battleford. Both names have been wiped out. A new riding named Battleford has been brought into existence, and the hon. member believes it will be Conservative. Two-thirds of the old riding of North Battle-ford has been called Redberry. In that riding the Grits are hived. place. The city of North Battleford is only a few miles from the boundary of Redberry riding, a riding which is made up as I have described. There are so many inaccuracies in the speech of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that I cannot let them go without challenge. In the first place the hon. member for Rosetown was not averse to his boundary going northward. In fact, I discussed the matter with him on more than one occasion. In the second place this map was not concocted in Regina. There was no committee in Regina I know of that had anything whatever to do with the map. It is true there was a meeting in Saskatoon and also one in Regina. I called in those who I believed knew the territory better than I did, and got their opinions. I received no instructions from them, but merely obtained their opinions as to the situation at each point. I did the same thing in connection with south Saskatchewan. I did not believe I would be doing my duty as a member of the committee if I did not get the information which was necessary, and upon which conclusions might be based. No member of the provincial legislature was at any of the meetings nor was the matter discussed with any member of the provincial legislature. I have had no communication directly or indirectly from any member of the legislative assembly in Saskatchewan with regard to the redistribution with the exception of two, and those members wrote me regarding the redistribution as it affected territory in which they themselves lived and no other territory. In neither case were their representations accepted by me. That is the extent to which any member of the provincial legislature had control over me concerning this committee. My hands were not tied by anybody; I came to it as a free agent to make this map in the way I thought fair, and have done my duty as I saw it. Hon. members who have listened to this debate so far and heard statements such as those made by the hon. member for North Battleford and the hon. member for Humboldt as to why they could 
not come to any arrangement with me, must now realize why it was absolutely impossible [DOT]for even the most reasonable men on this side of the house to get any reasonable settlement with gentlemen who have thus spoken, because they conducted themselves all through in the manner in which they are conducting themselves in this house now. With regard to the city of Saskatoon, it has grown by at least forty-eight per cent in the last ten years. The hon. member for Saskatoon has more confidence in his constituency than the hon. member for North Battleford has in his; he is not saying that people are going to leave because of inability to make a living in the constituency. I will do all the repeating that is necessary.

Then a statement is made in regard to consultation with Senator Willoughby. province of Saskatchewan. member for Melville a Liberal majority. I am going to ask that that injustice be rectified before we come to the schedules, and I am sure my hon. friend the member for Melville will have no objection.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING ((Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a number of hon. members from Saskatchewan have spoken already with regard to the province as a whole. I shall not go over ground that has been covered already, but, as the representative of one of the constituencies which is being materially altered in the schedules attached to the bill, I feel that on behalf of my constituents I should bring to the attention of the house and of the country just what is being attempted by the government under the proposed distribution. I believe this will serve as a good illustration of the sort of thing to which we on this side of the house are taking exception in the name of all that is fair and just.
It is a little difficult for one to distinguish between oneself as member for an individual constituency and as leader of a political party, but I am prepared to discuss the matter on both grounds, as to whether or not what is suggested with regard to Prince Albert is of a nature likely to commend itself to the sense of justice and fair play of the people of this country. The hon. member for Regina, who has spoken on behalf of the Conservative committee that arranged the bill so far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, said
[Mr. McPhee.3
that the problem was to readjust the constituencies along lines which would serve to bring them more into accord with the movement of the population to the north, and that it was necessary to take a constituency out from the southern part and add a constituency in the north. Perhaps for that general statement there is much to be said; just whether or not any question would arise from its operation would depend entirely upon from what place and in what manner the one constituency was removed and where the other constituency was added. The constituency which is being added in the north is to adjoin the constituency of Prince Albert, which I have the honour to represent in this house at the present time. The mind of the committee, which now must be the mind of the government since its recommendations form a part of the schedules as they appear in the bill, will I think be apparent from the figures which the committee had before it at the time the propopsed adjustment was made. The unit which, as I understand it, the committee sought to maintain as the (basis for constituencies in Saskatchewan was a representation of 44,186. This meant that constituencies having a larger representation should be reduced in size. Prince Albert came within that category; according to the figures before me, which I believe were before the committee, the present constituency of Prince Albert has a representation of 50,896. The problem then, in strict equity and justice, would be to reduce Prince Albert from 50,896 to 44,186, but what is the reduction that has been made? Prince Albert has been reduced to 38,469, and may I point out that it is only one of four constituencies of the twenty-two in Saskatchewan which now have units of less than 40,000.
When one comes to examine the other constituencies having representations of less than 40,000 one sees how this particular constituency of Prince Albert has been cut up in order to legislate out of his seat in this parliament the one who represents it at the present time and to help make absolutely secure at least one hon. gentleman who sits on the other side of the house. May I point out how the change that has been made, and in so doing I would say that this constituency, as redefined, is a fine exemplification of what is meant by the word "gerrymander." The word gerrymander in political parlance simply means that in redistributing a constituency the boundary lines are so altered as to do an obvious injury to one political party and give an obvious unfair political advantage to another party. According to the figures for

Re,distribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
the last general election in 1930 the constituency of Prince Albert gave me, as Liberal candidate, a majority of 1,192. Prince Albert is an old constituency which at one time elected Sir Wilfrid Laurier, at a general election many years ago. Later Sir Wilfrid decided to represent another constituency, to which he had also been elected, but Prince Albert has a certain tradition connected with the Liberal party, and for many years it has been a Liberal constituency. When I was without a seat following a general election of 1925, some 'hon. members from the province of Saskatchewan, together with others from other provinces, offered to place at my disposal their seats in the House of Commons in order that I might resume my duties here. The constituency of Prince Albert was mentioned as one which in all probability would give little concern to the leader of the Liberal party, as it was one of the recognized Liberal seats. In the same way I might say that the present Prime Minister, representing a constituency such as Calgary, may feel free to go from one end of Canada to the other during a political campaign without embassass-ment, because he represents a safe Conservative constituency. There was considerable chivalry on the part of hon. members on this side of the house when they came to offer their constituencies to their leader.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but I think the right hon. gentleman will recall that in 1911 the only constituency in Saskatchewan which returned a Conservative member was Prince Albert. It has not that Liberal tradition to which the right hon. gentleman refers.

That may have happened on one occasion, but I would point out that the representation of Prince Albert by two Liberal leaders, each of whom has held the office of Prime Minister of Canada entitles it to some place of special honour in the Liberal category, at any rate. Now let me point out what the change proposed today will mean, according to the figures of the last general election. If the last election had been fought within the boundaries proposed at present, instead of having a Liberal majority of 1,192 I would have been defeated by a Conservative majority of 618.
Hurrah!

Some hon.
gentleman says "hurrah"; that may be very chivalrous, but let me tell my hon. friends opposite that it is not in accord with the
sense of chivalry of the people of Canada, as a whole. It may be Tory chivalry but it is neither British chivalry nor British fair, play.
Cut it out.
I will not cut it out; I will say what I am called upon to say in reply to interruptions from hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is a lot more to say.

There is a good deal more to say. Now, may I ask how this has been brought about. It is very simple Those who had charge of the map havi looked over the constituency to see what portion of it gave the largest Liberal returns. They found that the southern portion did; they found that the southern portion had given a very considerable majority, and they have so altered the constituency as to take out of that southern portion a Liberal majority, of 1,719, which they have placed in a constituency they have newly framed to the south. The constituency which they have newly framed to the south is now being given a unit of 46,285, while they are reducing the unit of Prince Albert to 38,469. By taking this Liberal majority out, they have made the riding even smaller than the unit is according to the redistribution at the moment. What have they done in order to make the constituency what it now is? They have gone over into another constituency, the constits uency of Melfort, the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture, and taken a Tory section of his present constituency, which is to the east of Prince Albert, and added that to Prince Albert. They have not at any single place or in any single direction drawn a line which would be fair as between Liberals and Conservatives, but have taken out of and away from the south a part of the constituency strongly Liberal and to what remains they have added to the east a part of an adjoining constituency strongly Conservative. If there could be a clearer gerrymander of a constituency than that I should like to know what it is. I shall have a little more to say about this later on, but I cite what I do, as I wish to make it clear at the moment why it is that some of us on this side have found it impossible to agree to what has been proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite.
The hon. Minister of Public Works, speaking this morning of what there had been in the way of agreement among the different
5278	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Mackenzie King
provinces, said that some ninety per cent of the seats were already agreed upon. I am not admitting the truth of that, but supposing one were to admit that there is substantial agreement with respect to ninety per cent of the seats what follows: If there is injustice with respect to ten per cent, if the kind of thing that has been done in Prince Albert is repeated in ten per cent of the constituencies, it means that at least twenty-four of the constituencies are being altered unfairly through a gerrymander, in a way which will give to the government in power to-day an unfair advantage in the way of gain and the opposition the disadvantage to the- extent of almost certain defeat in these constituencies. With ten per cjent something like twenty-four constituencies, that represents a difference of forty-eight on a division. One can readily see wherein the will of the people is certain of defeat if the constituencies are gerrymandered in that way.
I submit that action of this sort is wholly indefensible, and I may perhaps be pardoned if I say I think it is doubly unchivalrous when it comes from a government towards the leader of the party opposing them. After all, there are some things one has a right to expect and to look forward to in public life; there are some amenities to be preserved between public men, and particularly men who have been in public life for a considerable time and in connection therewith have heavy responsibilities. I have taken the position from the start, with the members of the Saskatchewan committee, that I did not think the seat which I am representing at the present time in parliament should be brought into the discussion at all, but rather that I would look to the Prime Minister and the present government of Canada to do what they thought was fair and just by the leader of the opposition in this House of Commons, and one who, if I may be pardoned for saying so, has during the course of his leadership of his party held the office of Prime Minister for a period of nearly nine years. If they wish to legislate me out of my seat in parliament they can do it in this way. If I am to be thus prevented from coming back to continue to serve my country within the House of Commons, I have no doubt I shall outside the halls of parliament find plenty to do, to which I shall be able to turn with energy and zeal. But I believe that the people of Canada, whether Conservative or Farmer or Labour or Liberal, will resent a deliberate effort on the part of the government of the day, in virtue of its majority, to legislate out of his seat a political opponent who for many years 
has been the leader of his party. As I have said, I will leave to the Prime Minister and his colleagues the situation so far as this seat is concerned, and I may add that the Prime Minister cannot get away from his responsibility by saying that he knows nothing about this political map, having left it all to the hon. member for Regina to do with as he thinks best.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, to the committee.

Or to the committee either. The right hon. gentleman is Prime Minister and he has the final say in the matter. More than that, we all know that the members of the committee have been ' in constant conference with the Prime Minister himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not so.
Then I accept the right hon. gentleman's word.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have not been in
constant communication until after the difficulties arose.

I hope that
now difficulties have arisen the Prime Minister will accept some of his responsibility in this regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He is always ready and
willing to do so.

May I point
out what happened in 1923 at the time of our last redistribution. Those who were on the committee will recall the accuracy of what I say. I was then Prime Minister, charged with the responsibility which my right hon. friend has to-day. I was then representing another historic constituency, the constituency of North York. I was told that the committee had reached practical agreement with respect to most of the Ontario seats, but that there was one objection which was being raised by the Conservative party, namely, that the constituency of North York as it then stood had too small a unit of representation; it was felt that the unit of representation of that constituency ought to be enlarged. Had I wished to do so, I could as Prime Minister have intimated to the members of the committee that I hoped they would keep the unit of representation of North York just where it was. I knew what it meant, adding to the representation of North York, but I asked what would satisfy the committee as to the justice of the situation. They said they would like to have two townships added to North York-townships adjoining the city of Toronto. Hon. mem-

Redistribution-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
b-ers know what that would mean in the way of adding an increased Conservative following to the riding. I took the position that as Prime Minister I was not going to ask any favours for myself, or expect for the constituency I represented, anything which I would not ask equally for any other constituency. I said that if it was true that the representation of North York was small as compared with the others, then by all means these townships should be added. They were added, and when the general election came I carried the old constituency of North York but was defeated by the additional majority in the added constituency.
I take no pride in having adopted that attitude, but I have the satisfaction of knowing that I acted honourably in the matter, and I have nothing to regret with respect to my attitude toward any hon. gentleman opposite. If my hon. friends opposite do not wish to recognize any obligation of fairness, to say nothing of chivalry or justice, towards the leader of the party by which they are opposed, that is of course for themselves to decide. I am not at the moment pleading for myself, but I am speaking for the people of Prince Albert constituency, which has honoured me with its representation in this house, when I say that that constituency has the right to expect a unit of population equivalent to what is recognized as the unit of other constituencies in that province, and has the right to expect that if in a redistribution a change of its boundaries has to be made it will be made fairly as between Liberals and Conservatives in the riding as it stands at the present time.

If the declarations that are made now had been made when the committee started to sit some time ago they could have been taken as at least an indication of the intention to negotiate a redistribution map to a favourable conclusion. Judging from the negotiations which have taken place from the time we started until the time we concluded, in my opinion there was no intention on the part of Liberal Saskatchewan members to arrive at any concluded settlement unless it was absolutely upon their own terms.
That is not true.
That is absolutely untrue.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert is very much perturbed about the lack of chivalry due to the position of leader-
Due to any leader.

-whereby he might be legislated out of his seat in the province of Saskatchewan. In the first place at one stage in the proceedings I expressed to the hon. member for Humboldt some doubt as to whether the right hon. the leader of the opposition would be a candidate in Prince Albert at the next elections.

That is not for you to
decide.

May I say to my hon. friend that if I am not mistaken that observation was made some time ago by the Minister of Agriculture. The constituency of Prince Albert has now been so arranged as to bring his farm into it, evidently with a view to accommodating him.
May I ask the right hon. the leader of the opposition to give the statement he attributes to me.

Not so very long ago I received a communication from the Liberal committee of Prince Albert to the effect that my hon. friend had said that I would not run again in Prince Albert. They wanted to know whether that would be my decision. I replied that my decision would be to abide by the wish and will of my friends in Prince Albert, that if they wished me to run I would run, and that anything that might be said by others had no bearing on the situation so far as I was concerned.
Where do I come into the picture?

It was what my hon. friend said during the by-election in South Huron. A report was sent down to the constituency of South Huron that the leader of the opposition was not going to get a seat in Saskatchewan, that the next time he would not run in Prince Albert. We now begin to see what was evidently in the minds of those who were circulating the story.

While in Prince Albert I made no statement that the right hon. leader would not likely run in the federal constituency of Prince Albert during the next elections. As far as the by-election in South Huron is concerned, when discussing the matter on 'one of the platforms I stated that there were three questions for the electors to decide. One was the issues before the electorate, one had reference to the leaders of each party and the other concerned the candidates. I may have given the impression, which was no doubt in my mind at that time, that there would be little likelihood of the right hon. leader of the opposition running a*

Redistribution-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
a candidate in the constituency of Prince Albert. I gave my reasons for that, which the right hon. gentleman did not ask me. The right hon. leader of the opposition had done considerable travelling from one part of the country to the other as the result of which he had been elected in various constituencies throughout Canada from the east to the west.
I have given the reason why I was kept from North York.

To continue, when the right hon. the leader of the opposition first ran in Prince Albert constituency he had a majority of over five thousand. He spent a day and a half in the constituency between then and the next elections, and I believe his majority dropped by a little over fifteen hundred, or in the neighbourhood of five hundred for each half day or a thousand a day for each day he was in the constituency. I am just repeating now the substance of my remarks to one of the audiences to which I spoke. Between that and the next elections his majority dropped something in the neighbourhood of three thousand, which was a little over a thousand a day for each day the right hon. member had stayed in his constituency. With these facts in my mind I concluded that there was little likelihood of the right hon. member contesting the constituency in the next elections if he were forced to spend any time in the constituency.
The right hon. leader of the opposition made one statement referring to the will of the people to which I take exception, and if the committee will bear with me for a few minutes I think I can show that he is not correct in his statement. The last redistribution made it impossible for the people in the federal constituency of Prince Albert to express their will. I have before me the results of the last federal elections and they show that poll after poll in the northern part, and especially in the city of Prince Albert and the districts in the neighbourhood of Prince Albert, returned majority after majority against the right hon. gentleman. This is what happened in the Anglo-Saxon and French speaking part of the constituency and the only thing that enabled him to carry the election were the votes of a large block of people of German descent who had been left in the southern part of the seat in the last redistribution. I am not making any inference that these people should not be given every opportunity to exercise their franchise. They are of German descent. I had the privilege and pleasure of working throughout that whole district for years as a school inspector. Under the redistribution which was in force during the last

elections a large block of these people in the southern end of the Prince Albert constituency and another similar block to the north of Saskatoon, totalling in all about forty-five thousand progressive Mennonite farmers by being thus divided were practically denied the opportunity of nominating one of their own people so that this very worthy part of the Canadian population would be unable to express its opinion in this house. I know many of these people personally and they take second place to none, but this is what happened because of the work of scientific and highly specialized political racketeers. I do not think it was the work of the leaders of the Liberal party as we like to think of Liberalism. I believe it would have been a distinct gain it we could have as a member one of these people of German extraction who had made such a success. But that was made impossible because of the block left in Prince Albert constituency, evidently just to affect a vote of the people in the northern part of the constituency. By doing that, both these peoples have been practically disfranchised. The right hon. the leader of the opposition and his followers have therefore made it impossible for these people to express their will.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When I was speaking before six o'clock I was referring to the situation in Prince Albert. Until after the committee had reported, owing to the fact that there was a deadlock between the hon. member for Humboldt and myself regarding the method of redistribution rather than as to details with respect to seats, I received no information regarding what was wanted in Prince Albert other than the offer which I referred to in the letter which I read this afternoon, which offer was made in accordance with a conversation between the hon. member for Humboldt and myself. The hon. member for Humboldt says this afternoon that as well as delineating the southern boundary for Prince Albert he had stipulated that an angle south of the south branch of the Saskatchewan river should also have been removed from the Prince Albert constituency. As I said, I had no recollection of that, and my letter was written when the matter was very fresh in my memory and it contains no statement of that kind. In the reply made by the hon. member for Humboldt it was not mentioned as an essential feature of the offer, but

Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull
he simply said that the offer itself was wholly unacceptable. So there was no further discussion as to whether that feature had been eliminated or not.
That offer was refused, and I heard of no further offer until after the redistribution committee had reported, when I was presented with a map which retained the old boundaries of Prince Albert intact, and accompanying it was a request to divide the three constituencies of Yorkton, Last Mountain and Melville by a line running north and south instead of a line running east and west, thereby setting up the old seat of Melville again very close to the original plan; also a map subdividing the constituencies of North Battleford and South Battleford and sending South Battle-ford to the northern portion of the province. On that map the boundaries of ten constituencies were altered from the map that I had submitted. It is quite true that some of those alterations were minor alterations and were consequent upon the three major alterations to which I have referred in the Melville area, the Prince Albert area and the Battleford area. In that stage of the negotiations it was a rather big demand. I asked the hon. member for Humboldt to consult with his friends and come back to me and say what the minimum of his demand was in order to get a complete compromise on the Saskatchewan map. He came back and said that the reply was practically all that he had asked for in respect to these seats, and I replied that at that stage that was an impossible request from my point of view.
The right hon. leader of the opposition complains that in applying the principle of reducing the population of Prince Albert, which he now says was properly applied-and in the map presented by the other side of the house the population was also reduced but not down to the minimum between 45,000 and 46,000- I reduced his population too far, making it between 38.000 and 39,000, and he protests that it should have been left at at least 44,186. I submit that the leader of the opposition is not showing the acquaintance with his district that he ought to have. Quite a considerable number of people have gone into that constituency since the census of 1931 and that the addition of these people will bring the figure much more closely to the 44.000 unit than might be expected. It is further suggested that in arguing that the unit should not be below the average, no allowance is being made for the trends of population. Now the population in Saskatchewan as a whole, as is generally known, did not move north. That was not the cause of the maladjustment that I was attempting to remedy. The population in the southern part of the province grew just about as fast as it grew in the rest of Canada, but the population in the northern part grew very much faster. There was no great removal of population from the south to the north of the province prior to 1931. It was the excessive growth in the northern part of the province itself.

Will my hon.
friend allow me to make a correction, if it should be a correction. The figures that I gave as to the population of Prince Albert at present and the figures the committee had before them were based on the last census, not the figures that obtained at the time of the last election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The census figures?

The census
figures, yes.

I do not think there
is any dispute between us as regards that. The census gives 50,896 as the population in 1931. The population as proposed by the map submitted to me by the hon. member for Humboldt on the new basis would be 45,986, or within 14 of 46,000. The population I submitted was 38,469, and if the offer I had made in writing before referred to had been accepted, it would have added something like 6,400 or 6,500 to that population. But to ask now that the population of Prince Albert, or its boundaries shall remain intact, is not only to leave a population of nearly 51.000 in Prince Albert constituency but seriously to affect the adjustment in Melfort constituency as well. It would mean the transfer of 4,800 from Prince Albert to the Melfort district.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition says that I have apparently added insult to injury by carrying into his constituency from Melfort an area which gave a Tory majority at the last election. I am sorry if I have done that injustice to the Minister of Agriculture, because naturally he would feel very badly if he had lost any Conservative votes to the constituency of Prince Albert. My right hon. friend is very anxious lest we should legislate him out of his constituency. He talks a great deal about chivalry, with probably more heat than light. Out in our part of the country we merely call that "fanning the air." It does not weigh very heavily with the voters in Saskatchewan. I submit that there is not very much necessity to legislate the right hon. gentleman out of his seat. If he loses as many supporters between 1930 and the next election as he lost between 1926 and the last one it will take no legislation to remove him from Prince Albert.

Redistribution-Mr. Turnbull
In connection with these questions of chivalry, and chivalry especially to leaders of great parties in this country, it is well to remember what happened in the constituency of Portage la Prairie in 1924. Some additions were made at that time to the seat held by the then leader of the Conservative party. It is true that- by superhuman effort in 1925 the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen carried the seat. But it was one of the hardest seats in the province of Manitoba to get at, one of the hardest seats to work, and one which was calculated to defeat the right hon. leader of the Conservative party at that time- although in 1925 that purpose was not achieved. In 1926 it operated very much better, because not only did the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen lose his seat, but he abandoned his membership in the House of Commons. The people who did that are the people who in 1933 are talking about chivalry.
Apart from all the talk about fixing up a seat in Prince Albert for the right hon. leader of the opposition, let me say that the situation there is not entirely in line with anything which has happened heretofore. In the first place, that seat is not ordinarily the one held by the right hon. leader of the opposition. He came there more or less by political accident arising out of the previous election. He came there to find a safe refuge in the Prince Albert seat. Let me remind the committee that it would not have been a safe refuge, had it not been for the redistribution of 1924. The fixing of the boundaries of that constituency in 1924 made what was normally a seat with a fighting chance for both parties into an absolutely safe Liberal seat. The seat the right hon. gentleman represents was made safe by the redistribution of 1924. If we had been responsible for that redistribution we would have been accused of deliberate gerrymander. But for my right hon. friend it was merely a rearrangement of boundaries to suit the general welfare of the Dominion of Canada.

I hope my hon. friend will make it clear that the seat was one which had been carried by a Liberal member who resigned in my favour. It was not as the result of arrangement of any boundaries with a view to making a seat for myself.

Quite true, the right hon. gentleman was not a candidate in that constituency at the general election. I thought I had made that clear. The seat was won by Mr. McDonald by a very large majority, and after the redistribution of 1924. What I was trying to say was that by reason of the
[Mr. Turnbull.1
delineation of boundaries which took place in 1924 Prince Albert became a safe Liberal seat, and because it was a safe Liberal seat it offered a refuge for the right hon. gentleman when he lost his election in an Ontario constituency. Since the right hon. gentleman went to Prince Albert as a result of a political misfortune in another province, there is no guarantee that at any time it will be a permanent seat for him. He is not in the same position as is my right hon. leader in the city of Calgary. Calgary has been his home for many years. Again, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen had been for many years a resident of Portage la Prairie. It might be, if Prince Albert has been fixed up as now suggested, that at the time of an election the right hon. leader of the opposition might find a seat in Ontario or Prince Edward Island, and we would be faced with the proposition of placing another Liberal candidate in Prince Albert, a seat made safe by reason of operations which took place in 1924.
If time permitted and if I considered it worth while I could point out seat after seat in the province of Saskatchewan which was fixed up in 1924, even though the late Senator Willoughby was consulted. The map speaks for itself. There is no question about it, that whether it was intended or not the result of the redistribution of 1924 was to make that province much safer for Liberals than it had been before the redistribution. I do not quarrel with my hon. friends for that. I merely ask them, knowing what was done in 1924, not only in the province of Saskatchewan but in other Canadian provinces, not to trouble us with their mock heroics regarding misfortunes which they say they are suffering in 1933. There are plenty other seats in Saskatchewan which are perfectly safe Liberal seats. I think there is cause to apply the same principle to the constituency of Prince Albert as was applied to other seats in the northern part of the province, that is to say, reduce the population below the unit, taking into consideration the .fact that the trend of increased population is to the northern part of the province and that in the last ten years that constituency has grown up by thirty per cent. After due allowance is made for that, it is found that the population is between 38,000 and 39,000 which is ample population for that particular seat at the moment. Not only that, but the justice of what I say is shown by the maps submitted to me by the hon. member for Humboldt. I am not charging him with the responsibility for drawing the map, but I say that the map submitted to me by him removed some fifteen townships from the southern part of

Redistribution-Mr. Totzke
the seat of Prince Albert. That is I think approximately what -would have been removed had the boundary I offered been accepted. If it was a great injustice for me to move those townships from Prince Albert, what must it have been for a member of the committee on the other side of the house. Lest someone may make a mistake about a township, may I explain that townships in the eastern part are different from those in the west. Out west a township is six miles square or thirty-six square miles. Ffteen of those townships, according to the map presented by the hon. member for Humboldt, were to be removed from the southern part of the constituency. So there was not very much difference there. The Liberal map, if we may call it such, provided for a reduction of population, as well. Not only that, the redistribution of 1924 placed those three northern seats below the unit for the western provinces, and I was merely following that precedent upon this occasion.
With regard to the so-called serious trouble in Battleford, and the complaint that Battle-ford was not made Battlefords, the fact of the matter is that in the draft of the boundaries which went to the printer the word Battle-fords appeared, but in the printing the "s" was dropped out. If it would relieve the mind of the hon. member for North Battleford I may tell him that I shall move at the proper time that the letter " s " be restored, and that both Battlefords be recognized in the future history of Saskatchewan, as reflected in this redistribution.
May I say in conclusion that I regret very much the hon. member for Humboldt and myself were from the start so vastly separated on a question of principle that I was not able to get the cooperation from him on details that I otherwise would have had. The question of a boundary line being a little too far one way or another was one which might have been ironed out, had there been cooperation between us on other points. But in view of the fact that the hon. member for Huim-boldt would not relent unless I abandoned the plan of cutting out a seat and putting in another which I had in view, there was no possibility of our getting together on details. We could have got together on details had I accepted his map. That was dear from the start. But I look upon that as being dictated to by the brute force of a minority, if one wished to use that term in connection with the righteous actions of the house. When it comes to a question of small changes here and there in boundaries I quite readily admit that a boundary might have been placed a mile east or west of where I would put it and one
point might be as satisfactory as the other.
I am sorry the admission of the right hon. member for Prince Albert did not come earlier in the negotiations to the effect that it did not matter very much whether a seat was cut out in the centre and a new one formed in the north, but it mattered where it was cut out and where the new one was added. Had that position been taken by hon. members opposite at an earlier stage in the negotiations Saskatchewan might have been much more nearly united at the close of those negotiations than it is now. May I say, however, that out of the twenty-one seats in Saskatchewan there is a pretty substantial amount of agreement in respect to seventeen. We are not so very far apart, in the end. If we were able to achieve that amount of agreement it seems to me that all the hysterics about deliberate gerrymanders and unfairness and all that sort of thing which we have had thrown at us, has not much solid basis in fact.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to follow my hon. friend from Regina through all his statements. The personal and racial atmosphere was not introduced into this debate until the hon. Minister of Agriculture took a hand this afternoon. But I want to dissociate myself from the position that the hon. member for Regina has tried to put me in. He has tried his utmost to fix on me the onus of having placed the constituency of my leader in the state in which it is now found. He said I had never at any time objected very strongly to the constituency of Price Albert as proposed. He must admit, however, that every map I proposed to him showed the boundary of Prince Albert extending to the town of Rosthern. It is true that some townships were taken off the southeastern corner of the constituency, but it was done because we wanted to live up to the principle we were working on of more nearly equalizing the population. The hon. member for Regina was most emphatic until near the end of the negotiations that the southern boundary as placed on his map must stay there. He also insisted that that portion taken from the Melfort seat and put into Prince Albert should remain. He now explains that he must apologize to the hon. member for Melfort for taking these good Tory votes and putting them into Prince Albert. I know very well why it was done. To-day we have seen what was in the mind of the hon. gentlemen; they thought they were going to force the leader of the opposition out of the constituency of Prince Albert and make him run elsewhere.
Redistribution-Mr. Totzke

My hon. friend said he had reason to believe that the leader of the opposition was not going to run in Prince Albert. He mentioned that to me once; I think it was about the time of the election in South Huron. He will remember I told him, when the rumour came from Prince Albert that the right hon. leader of the opposition was not going to run there, that my leader himself immediately made the statement that as long as the people of Prince Albert wanted him to represent them he was going to do so.
Will my hon. friend permit a question? Did the line that he and I agreed upon, which was marked upon the map, include within the constituency of Prince Albert the town of Rosthem?

There my hon. friend, I will not say intentionally, is again misrepresenting my attitude. We did not agree on that line. It was after the hon, member had told me that he certainly could not admit an alteration of the southern boundary that I tried to get from him an indication as to how far he would go. He said he would consider this. Every time I asked him for an alteration in the boundaries of a constituency the only thing that I could get was that he would consider it.
Did you not get an offer in writing?
To consider it?
No, an offer of the boundary in writing.

Nothing very definite. But I will say this, that every time I submitted a map to him, even when we were trying the hardest to equalize the population in the northern constituencies as he wished them, the town of Rosthern was always included in any map submitted. It is not fair on the part of the hon. member to try to hang on me the accusation that I was endeavouring in any way to limit the chances of my leader in the constituency of Prince Albert. Besides, I was not specially concerned at the moment about the constituency of Prince Albert, because I felt sure that the Prime Minister would not see an injustice done to the leader of the opposition. I had an assurance later on from a member of the government that nothing would be done to legislate the leader of the opposition out of his seat in Prince Albert. It is true that the last map that I submitted, which I could not get the committee of elder statesmen to allow me to argue before them, had alterations in some of the constituencies- the hon. member for Regina says in ten; I

did not count them-but these were necessary on account of the alterations in Melville and north of Melville.
I mentioned a moment ago the remarks made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon. He is running true to form. The first session he came down here he told us and told the people of Saskatchewan that he was not a politician, that he did not know anything about the game. That first session thoroughly proved that he was not a politician, and to-day proves it again. This is the first time in the proceedings, either here or in the committee, that the political or racial question has been brought into the debate in any shape or form. The hon. Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon that the right hon. leader of the opposition was elected in Prince Albert not by those of Anglo-Saxon origin but by those in the southern portions of the constituency which are populated predominantly by men of German origin. He said the Anglo-Saxon people of Prince Albert constituency were disfranchised-and this from a member of a government sworn to His Majesty to serve loyally and truly the people of this dominion! If any people of Prince Albert, Mr. Chairman, were disfranchised by the votes cast by the people of the southern part of the district, I would protest in the strongest language of which I am capable. He said that is the reason that the southern portion of Prince Albert constituency was taken from that constituency and put in a new one, so that they could be with their own class and would have an opportunity to elect one of themselves.
Before I make any further comment in that regard, may I say that the people of Rosthern district to my knowledge are very anxious that the leader of the opposition shall again represent them in the next parliament. The hon. Minister of Agriculture knows that constituency-he admitted that this afternoon___
knows it very well. He inspected the schools through there; he inspected the schools in my own community, and when he says that the new constituency is composed of people almost entirely of the same class as those around Rosthern and that the southern portion of Prince Albert which is being removed was predominantly populated by these people, I want to call to his attention the names of many places in that district; he knows them well, and he will know the class of people who live there. For example listen to these names: Domremy, Duck Lake-you will remember Duck Lake from the 1885 rebellion days.

Redistribution-Mr. Totzke
Those are not in the southern part of the constituency of Prince Albert.
They certainly are.
My whole point this afternoon was the solid block of Mennonites amounting to 40,000.
My hon. friend knows very well that these places I have mentioned-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The old stuff.

You remember Batoche and Fish Creek. My hon. friend says they are a bunch of foreigners. Are you going to call people who are Canadianized or were born in Canada foreigners? Are you going to call the French people who settled there many years ago foreigners? Domremy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is running true to form.
St. Louis, St. Isidore de Bellevue-are those likely to be German settlements?
Those are not in the southern part.
They are, every one of them.
Mr. Chairman, I object to being interrupted in this way. The Minister of Agriculture is not adding anything to the debate. He simply says they are not in the southern part; I say they are.
It is a matter of geography.

These are French communities. Then I have another list of names which are neither Anglo Saxon nor German. Let me read this list: Blaine Lake; Petrofka, and St. Julien. That sounds French, but it is settled largely by Ukrainians. Then there is Wakaw, settled by Ukrainians and Hungarians, and we have the German settlements, Waldheim, Laird and Rosthem, and there are one or two other little places also. These are in the southern portion of the constituency of Prince Albert as it now exists. They are south of Duck lake, so that town must be in the constituency of Prince Albert also.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that I very much regret that this matter has been brought into the house. I want to say, however, that I know the people in those constituencies; I have the honour of representing a number of similar people, and I am very proud to
do so. There are no more loyal Canadians than these people, and I resent any imputations against their loyalty to their adopted country. They do not want to be hived by themselves; they want to take their position as Canadian citizens, and they want to assume their rights and privileges with all the responsibilities that go with them. This shows what hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to do. They are attempting to keep the Anglo-Saxons together and to put those of foreign extraction off by themselves, because they know that most of these people who have taken up residence in this country are not bound by the traditions of eastern Canada or the mother country, but have been able to figure out for themselves just what party they wish to support. I was going to remark here that if the speech made this afternoon by my hon. friend is similar to the speeches he made during the by-election in South Huron I am not at all surprised that my hon. friend from South Huron was returned with such a substantial majority.

He knows the people there; he has inspected schools all through that district, and he will recognize the names I am going to mention. How about Alvena? That is not a German community; it is settled almost entirely by Ukrainians and their descendants, and a very good class of people they are too. How about Aberdeen? In that he was quite right.
I was told that the committee had reached a practical agreement with respect to most of the Ontario seats but that there was one objection which was being raised by the Conservative party, namely that the constituency of North York as it then stood had a small unit of representation, and it was felt that the unit of representation of that constituency ought to be enlarged. Had I wished to do so, I could as Prime Minister have intimated to the members of the committee that I hoped they would keep the unit of representation of North York just where it was. I knew what it meant, adding to the representation of North York, but I asked what would satisfy the committee as to the justice of the situation. They said they would like to have two additional townships added to North York-townships adjoining the city of Toronto. Hon. members know what that would mean in the way of adding an increased Conservative following to the riding. I took the position that as Prime Minister I was not going to ask any favours for myself or expect for the constituency I represented anything which I would not ask equally for any other constituency. I said that if it was true that the representation of North York was small as compared with the others, then by all means these townships should be added. They were added, and when the general election came I carried the old constituency of North York but was defeated by the additional majority in the added constituency.
I take no pride in having adopted that attitude, but I have the satisfaction of knowing that I acted honourably in the matter, and I have nothing to regret with respect to my attitude to any hon. gentleman opposite.
Let me ask the house to bear with me while I discuss the political complexion of these two townships which the right hon. gentleman says the Conservative desired to have added to the old North York and to which he, in a moment of weakness apparently, consented.
I cannot go back prior to 1925, because prior to that, in the two preceding elections in North York, there were three candidates. Now let us see what a great sacrifice the right hon. the leader of the opposition made.

speechtext:
I rise merely to correct
a misstatement made this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman, because, to use his own words, it is always desirable that the record should be historically correct. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was never a candidate in Prince Albert. That is No. 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was never a candidate in Prince Albert.
In what is now the constituency of Prince Albert.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, never. Secondly, it is not traditionally Liberal. Here is the record. 1 thought I remembered very distinctly what the position was when I went west but I have taken the trouble during the recess to get the Parliamentary Guide and at page 278 the record of Prince Albert is given. It came into being in 1908. At the first general election Mr. Rutan, a Liberal, was elected, and he was the member for three years until in 1911 the seat was carried by Mr. James McKay, a Conservative. He remained until at a by-election the next year Mr. Donaldson, a Conservative, was elected in his place. The seat then remained Conservative until 1917, when the government candidate, Mr. Knox, was elected by a majority of 3,590. Mr. Knox was an opponent of the Liberals at that time. He was reelected as a Progressive in 1921, and the seat remained Progressive until 1925 when Mr. McDonald was elected, and he was succeeded on his retirement by the right hon. leader of the opposition, who is still the member for that constituency. A note is appended, "See Assiniboia, and particularly the reference under that head to the old electoral division of Saskatchewan."
At page 217 of the Parliamentary Guide is the record of Saskatchewan. The record with respect to Saskatchewan is as follows, Saskatchewan being an electoral division that returned one member only for the whole of the territorial division of Saskatchewan.
Of which Prince Albert was an important part.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. there were several
places, including Saskatoon, then an embryo city.
In 1906? Oh, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am making my observations from this record, and at page 218 is the record of this traditionally Liberal seat! In 1887, at the first election, Mr. Maedowall, a Conservative, was elected by 166. He was reelected in 1891 by 283, and in 1896 Sir Wilfrid Laurier was elected by 44. But I find that he was also elected in the same election for Quebec East, and that he resigned his seat at Prince Albert and was succeeded by Mr. T. 0. Davis, Liberal, who was reelected in 1900, and when he went to the Senate he was succeeded in 1904 by Mr., now Mr. Justice, Lamont, a Liberal. So it is not a traditionally Liberal seat, and secondly, Sir Wilfrid Laurier never sat for Prince Albert, and never was elected for Prince Albert.

He was elected.



Redistribution-Mr. Bennett

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Never was elected. He was elected for what is known as the electoral division of Saskatchewan. When I went west there were four ridings in the northwest territories: Alberta, represented by Mr. Oliver, West Assiniboia, represented by Mr. Davin, East Assiniboia, represented by Mr. Douglas and later by Mr. Turriff, and the other was Saskatchewan, which in 1896 was represented by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was succeeded by Mr. Davis when Sir Wilfrid elected to sit for Quebec East.
That is the record. I do not think for a single moment that the right hon. gentleman deliberately misstated it, but it just shows how one may for a moment have in one's mind an idea that is hardly consonant with the exact facts, just as the right hon. gentleman had with respect to his position in North York. It turns out as a matter of fact that had it not been for the two townships that were added by the redistribution of 1924 he would have been beaten by a much larger majority than he was. I am not for a moment asserting that he made the misstatement deliberately. It is just one of those accidents that sometimes happens to one's memory, and I merely correct the misstatement in order that the record may be historically correct.
That is why it is done- statesmanlike.

He said that he did not
know whether the misrepresentations were wilful or not. He qualified his statement.

My statement was to the effect that in the southern portion of the constituency of Prince Albert at the present time there were people of German descent. I maintain that that is correct. Here are the names of some of the places: Laird, Waldheim, and Rosthem, which are practically solidly German, and then north of Saskatoon are Hepburn, Hague, Mennon, Langham, Osier and Dalmeny, practically all solid German. The statement that I endeavoured to make was that by virtue of these people being placed as they were in a block in Prince Albert, and similarly to the north of Saskatoon city, it was practically impossible for them to

nominate one of their own people. As to referring to them in any way as foreigners or people who are not loyal to Canadian institutions, I went out of my way, and there is no distance to which I would not go, to uphold these people as Canadian citizens. But I do not know of any instance in my memory in which any hon. member in this house or out of it went further than the hon. member for Humboldt when he tried by the greatest stretch of imagination to suggest that I considered that the French were foreigners.
I did not say that.

I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member has accused me of saying that the French-Canadians in that constituency were foreigners. I did not say that. I said he had said these people of German extraction in the southern portion of Prince Albert were being put into the new seat so they would be with people of their own kind. I made no statement as to them being classed as foreigners.
