I wish to repeat that I did not say the hon. member had referred to French-Canadians as foreigners. I distinctly said, with regard to his remarks in connection with moving the people of German extraction from the southern portion of Prince Albert into this new seat which was being created, that it was for the purpose of putting them with people of their own kind, in order that they might be able to nominate one of their own people to represent them in this House of Commons. I was simply showing that they were not the same kind of people as those to which he had referred in the southern portion of Prince Albert. In that portion of Saskatchewan the people do not wTant to be put into situations of that kind. They want to live together in peace and harmony. They do live together in peace and harmony out there. They are among the best citizens of Canada, and the younger generation are growing up to love this country as their own. If at any time anything disparaging is said in this house eencerning those people I for one will be on my feet to defend them to the best of my ability.

It has been amusing to sit in this committee from eleven o'clock this morning and to listen to the words of hon. members opposite concerning that which they have been pleased to term the gerrymandering of 1032-33. While perhaps it may be very elevating to hear the expressions of high idealism from broadminded men who wish to redistribute the constituencies of Canada so that they will be perfectly fair to all members, one is led to wonder how fragile the memories of hon. members opposite must be. The hon. member for Regina referred to what took place in the constituency of Portage la Prairie in an effort to defeat the election to the House of Commons of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. It was my privilege to go through that elongated constituency and to see for myself some of the things that were done. If the right hon. gentleman who has bewailed so bitterly what has taken place in Prince Albert would obtain a map of the province of Manitoba as it was prepared in the redistribution of 1923-24, he would see how far his idealism and chivalry to opponents carried him at that time.
To my personal knowledge the same agent who went out from the city of Ottawa to the 53719-334J
constituency of Portage la Prairie to arrange that redistribution passed through all the constituencies in northern Ontario. I had the privilege of meeting the gentleman in my home town, although he did not know to whom he was talking at the time. He was accompanied by other political leaders of the north, members from the Timiskamings, East and West Algoma and Port Arthur. If the right hon. gentleman wishes to know where the word "gerrymander" really got its pernicious meaning he should come to northern Ontario and I will show him. I will show him what took place in 1924. If hon. members opposite want to know where the hon. member who invented the jig saw puzzle obtained his ideas, let them come to northern Ontario, and they will find out.
Where?
In Timiskaming.
Not in Timiskaming; I object to that.

Let the hon. member possess his soul in peace for a few moments, and I shall show him what took place in South Timiskaming in 1924. Why did a change take place? Because this gentleman who went out from the city of Ottawa had specific instructions to make the Timiskamings safe, regardless of what he did. "Make it impossible to elect a member in East Algoma. Hive the Tories in West Algoma, and make it impossible to elect a Conservative member in Port Arthur." If the committee will bear with me I will read some of the descriptions from the statute passed as a result of that redistribution. Let us first take West Algoma:
Algoma West consisting of those parts of the territorial districts of Algoma and Sudbury . . .
Note the expression "the territorial districts of Algoma and Sudbury." We have heard some discussions this afternoon with regard to members having to go fifty, sixty or seventy miles out of their way to reach parts of their constituencies. Let me indicate what is involved in the designation I have read. We find the term "parts of the territorial districts of Algoma and Sudbury." In order for the hon. member for AVest Algoma to get into the district of Sudbury he has to cross the district of East Algoma. There is no point in West Algoma which was contiguous, within one hundred miles, to the district of Sudbury. And to reach the points within the district of Sudbury which were taken out of East Algoma and added to AVest Algoma and, in order to carry out the instruction to make it impossible for a Conservative member to be elected in East Algoma, what did the hon. member for

Redistribution-Mr. Nicholson
West Algoma have to do? He had to travel one hundred and seventy-two miles, one hundred and sixty of which were in East Algoma or in Nipissing, going southwesterly all the time. Then he had to travel one hundred and seventy-two miles northwesterly to reach that point which it was desired should be taken out of East Algoma. But there were other points in East Algoma which were to be put in with West Algoma, and in order for the hon. member for West Algoma to reach them he had to go back one hundred and seventy-two miles, travel up the Canadian Northern railway one hundred and eighty miles through parts of the district of Nipissing-South Timiskaming, as it was gerrymandered into in 1924-and East Algoma.
Let me follow that up. This is the further designation with regard to West Algoma-I shall not read the whole of it 'because it takes nearly a whole page in the statutes:
. . . the township of Dowsley, thence east along the north boundary of the township of Dowsley to the northeastern boundary of the township of Ebbs, thence south along the east boundary of the township of Ebbs to the northwestern boundary of the township of Doherty, thence east .along the northern boundary of the township of Doherty to the northeastern boundary of the township of Shanley but not including the village of Horne-payne.
Perhaps this is the illustration that will best indicate the chivalry and fairness that was exercised in the 1924 redistribution. The village of Hornepayne lies completely inside the township and within the district of West Algoma. But it comprised a population that it was thought could be influenced to vote Liberal, while in the rest of the township was a population that might vote Conservative. They could not get a sieve fine enough to run these two groups of people through and get the Liberals into Port Arthur and the Conservatives into West Algoma, so they picked up the village of Hornepayne and transferred it to Port Arthur. But thpy did not stop there. There was a part of West Algoma known as Michipicoten harbour and Michipicoten island, all within the district and constituency of West Algoma, about eighty miles by boat from the Soo, and containing such places as the Helen mine and Goudreau, by rail about 150 miles within the border of West Algoma. But there were some voters there who it was thought might be transferred to Port Arthur and influenced to vote there, so they too were transferred to Port Arthur. I will not stop to read them all. To get to that part of his constituency the hon. member for Port Arthur had either to charter a vessel and travel 350 miles down lake Superior or to travel 380 miles by rail.

Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? As he is discussing Timiskaming I assume he is familiar with the map as drawn at present. Is it not a fact that North Timiskaming is left exactly as it was in the 1924 redistribution, and South Timiskaming is left as it was with a very slight exception?

Either the hon. gentleman was not listening or I succeeded very badly in making myself clear. I was referring to South Timiskaming, East Algoma, West Algoma and Port Arthur. These were the four constituencies about which specific instructions were issued and to which special agents were sent right from Ottawa in 1924. Let me come back to that point about Michipicoten harbour and island, with about 180 voters that were transferred from West Algoma to Port Arthur-why? In the hope that a Conservative member could not be elected in Port Arthur; and they were taken out of West Algoma in order to increase the majority of my hon. friend the present member for West Algoma. As I stated, the member for Port Arthur had to travel 380 miles by rail to reach these points, of which the last 130 miles were through the territory of West Algoma.
Now I will just come to South Timiskaming. First of all the description starts:
-consisting of that part of the territorial district of Timiskaming . . .
And then further down:
-and that part of the territorial district of Sudbury-
Now, what is it necessary for a member representing South Timiskaming to do in order to get into that part of the territorial district of Sudbury, and why was that change made? Nipissing in 1921 had a majority of almost

When Algoma was divided after the 1901 census the line between West and East Algoma ran straight north from Georgian bay. But it happened that the member for East Algoma from 1917 to 1921 lived in that part of the riding where he has lived for the whole of his adult life. He happened to be interested in three fairly large saw mills employing from 1,000 to 1,500 men all the year round, and living thereabouts. Something had to be done to correct a situation of that kind. The Conservative member lived there; the Conservative candidate lived there. That would never do. So they ran this line to the south boundary of the 21st range of townships and thence east along the said south boundary to a point directly south of the southeast corner of the township of Lackner. What did they do by that? They simply took out four little towns in three townships, the town of Chapleau, in which I live, and Devon, Nicholson and Dalton, where my saw mills, or those in which I am interested, are, and where the people I employ happen to live. That is what my right hon. friend will designate as chivalry towards political opponents, the high idealism that demands that constituencies be distributed fairly and equally amongst representatives in the House of Commons. I commend the ideal, Mr. Chairman; that certainly is the attitude that should prevail, but I just ask my right hon. friend to search his memory and ask his friends who were on that committee to search their memories and recall the instructions that were given to the solicitor in the city of Ottawa who traversed these constituencies east and west and stopped off at all points of interest to see what could be done to gerrymander members out of their seats, and then make another speech and tell the 'house what a real gerrymander is. We used to hear of Sir John Macdonald stating in answer to Sir Richard Cartwright regarding gerrymanders that if he lived another ten years he would gerrymander him again. And I 'have no doubt that if my right hon. friend were to have the opportunity ten years from now he would gerrymander again. Taking
the picture I know to have existed in northern Ontario and realizing what was done, Sir John Macdonald would consider himself as a gerrymanderer to be a perfect piker, to use the common phrase; he would say, "I know nothing about the task, refer me to those who committed that gerrymander of 1924."

I am rather glad my hon. friend has turned the discussion to- the province of Ontario. This afternoon and evening we have listened with a great deal of patience to a discussion of the redistribution of seats in the province of Saskatchewan. I feel that something should be said with regard to what I consider to be the greatest unfairness in representation in any province of the Dominion of Canada, that is, the disproportion of representation in the province of Ontario. The bill we are considering is the result of the meditations of a committee of hon. members of this house, who I think have worked laboriously for some time. That there is decided disagreement on the part of members of the committee none will deny, and to me the cause of that disagreement is quite apparent. From the discussion during the time the committee was sitting, as well as the . discussion to which we have listened here, it seems to me that personal considerations for members of this house, as well as political considerations, have taken up altogether too much time, while the consideration of fair representation for the municipalities has not been given enough time. After all it is our duty, whether we be in this house or on a committee, to follow the British North America Act and every ten years, after the decennial census, to try to rearrange the ridings of the dominion so that the voters will have a fair say, and not so that those now in parliament will have safe seats. After this parliament is over not a single one of us will have a seat or any claim on one; the most we will have will be the right to represent some party at the polls and to ask the people for their suffrage. I am not a particle interested in whether the last distribution was as bad as this distribution; the fact remains that the committee did come to an agreement.

My right hon. friend says there was some difference, but certainly this redistribution, as I am prepared to show, is just about as bad as it could be if you are thinking of the rights of the electors in the province of Ontario. I have compiled two or three sets of figures to which I should like to refer. The average of population in the

ridings in Ontario should be about 40,000. But while it is fair that one man should have as much say in the administration of the country as another man there is another factor in addition to population which must not be ignored, and that is the number of votes polled. I believe the men who think enough of their franchise to go to the polls have a greater right to consideration than those who do not vote. There is also the question of the geographic problems in some of the very large ridings. Therefore every redistribution committee has to agree to some extent that the urban population, which does not vote in the same percentage as the rural population, should have a larger unit of population than the rural seats.
Is the hon. gentleman referring only to the province of Ontario now?
I am dealing with the province which I represent.
That is not correct so far as our province is concerned.

It has been generally agreed in the province of Ontario that a smaller unit of population in the rural districts was fair for the reason that it was easier for the candidates to work a city seat, and also because in a city riding not such a large percentage of the voters come out on polling day. Even allowing for these factors, may I point to a few cases and ask where any fairness exists in regard to the unit of population? I see my hon. friend from Lincoln sitting opposite. Lincoln takes in the town of St. Catharines and a very prosperous farming area surrounding it. The riding of Kent takes in the city of Chatham and the very prosperous country surrounding it. These ridings, along with North Waterloo-which takes in the city of Kitchener and a very rich agricultural district-each have about 53,000 electors, and they each poll in the neighbourhood of 35,000 votes. On the other hand, in the centre of this province we have two members from the county of Brant and the city of Brantford. The county of Brant polled only 9,000 votes, while the city of Brantford polled 15,000 votes. So it takes two citizens of Lincoln or Kent or North Waterloo to equal one citizen in the county of Brant. I see my hon. friend from Kingston opposite; his is a purely city riding with 26,000 electors, just half the number in some of the other seats in the province.
I must say that bearing these facts in mind this seems an unfair redistribution. I am not blaming the members of the committee at all; I am blaming every man in this house. The chairman of the committee may reply 
that this is what we did at the last redistribution, but that is no excuse for doing it a second time. Here we have ridings like Kingston, with 26,000 voters, polling 11,000 votes; Brantford with 32,000 voters polling
15.000	votes; Toronto East with 69,000 voters polling 19,000 votes, and Toronto South, with
46.000	voters, only polling 7,000 votes. Then we have the township of Brant with 21,000 voters polling 9,000; North and South Bruce, with 21,000 or 22,000 voters polling 10,000 or
11.000	votes. In contrast we have the district of Nipissing, in a part of Canada which is growing rapidly due to the expansion of the mining industry. Under this bill there will be 70,000 people in that constituency, and at the last election they polled 23,000 votes. I agree with my hon. friend from East Algoma that the difficulties in such ridings as the Algomas and the Nipissings are very great; the people are scattered along the railway line and candidates must travel many miles in order to get to their constituents. At the same time the Algomas have 37,000 or 38,000 people, which is a bit too much having regard to the physical and geographic problems which exist.
I have no complaint to make with regard to the taking away of a seat from the counties of Grey and Bruce, making three seats instead of four. As a result of that division the representation of these seats will be from 32,000 to 35,000. I do submit, however, this one thought: While it is perfectly fair to put the unit of representation in my county at 35,000 I am far from satisfied when I see another county smaller than mine, which a candidate can cover in two hours in an automobile left unchanged while I must travel 120 miles to cover the length of my riding, and must use horse-drawn vehicles during some seasons of the year.
I believe that this redistribution in Ontario -and I have said this to my hon. friend from West Middlesex who represented the party to your left, Mr. Chairman-should have brought about a greater change in order to give a more equitable distribution of the voting power of this province. After all I think we are doing too much counting what the results of the 1926 and 1930 elections happened to be; we are wasting too much time counting up what various townships gave in Conservative, Liberal or Progressive votes. As I see it our task is to try to get some equality in regard to representation, and as representatives of the people I hardly think it is good enough for us to be satisfied providing the redistribution suits certain members of the house and makes certain seats safe. I think if the Ontario committee had really wanted to do so it could have made ten or twenty changes which would have brought the average unit close to 40,000

Redistribution-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
instead of having the list start at the top with
18.000	in some ridings and wind up at the bottom of the list with ridings like Welland, with 82,000, and Nipissing with 70,000. It does seem to me that the public have a right to a more equitable representation than they are getting. I would say also, that the representation of a riding with five votes on the list for every vote polled would not justify putting two seats in this riding. It just happens that the ridings which in my opinion are worst sinned against are the ridings in which the people poll a very large percentage of the votes on the list.
Someone, I believe the hon. member for Bast Algoma, was speaking a little while ago as to what had taken place in the last redistribution. I hardly think there has been a sufficiently marked change to indicate that the last redistribution could have been quite as bad as the hon. gentleman almost suggests it was. A great many of these seats in Ontario are fairly well represented; with respect to probably two thirds of them one can take no particular exception because they are as close to the unit of population as they can be while still preserving county boundaries. But I do submit to the chairman of the committee and to the house that as between, on the one hand, fully 8 or 10 seats in Ontario which are polling only 8,000 or 9,000 votes, and on the other hand 8 or 10 seats which are polling from
22.000	to 25,000 votes, there is a gulf which does not indicate very good work on the part of this or of past redistribution committees. I suggest that now this matter is before the house for consideration we should be well advised to observe county boundaries more fully than we have done, to increase representation in a good many of the districts which are overpopulated and to make some changes in those which are under-populated.

My memory is good and I can substantiate what I say. Now, there never 'has been a redistribution that has followed exactly the underlying principles which we all say should be adopted. There never has been a redistribution satisfactory to all concerned. Take each and every one of them and you will find just as glaring discrepancies as my hon. friend has pointed out to-night.
There is no province in Canada with as bad a spread in representation as Ontario, from 20,000 to 70,000.

Quite so, and the biggest spread.	[DOT]

My hon. friend knows that the urban population has created a problem which is difficult to deal with. On the one hand we have the contention that you must not decrease rural representation, and on the other hand we have the contention that you must increase the urban representation. We have endeavoured to keep both these in mind and to give to cities an increase, though not such as they desire, while not disturbing too greatly county boundaries or conditions as we find them. Particularly have we endeavoured to avoid tearing up the map, as it were, where it had been all torn up only ten years ago and the electors in those areas which had been then disturbed had just got quietly settled down and had adapted themselves to the changed conditions. This has been described as a gerrymander, but let me say to my hon. friends that I have no confidence in gerrymanders. I do not believe either of the parties think that you can count on any definite advantage being gained in an election from a redistribution. I think the results of the last redistribution proved that quite clearly. In 1925, following the last redistribution, the advantages were certainly not in our favour. We went to the country with fifty members and came back with 117.
I think it is perfectly clear that in these days and in these peculiar times you cannot count with any accuracy upon the results of a readjustment. After all, public opinion prevails. If my hon. friends think that as far as I am concerned or as far as this committee is concerned in this redistribution we have been primarily and principally concerned in endeavouring to secure some small, petty party advantage, which I think we will all agree is extremely doubtful, then they are absolutely mistaken. I ask my hon. friends to appreciate the difficulties which confronted

Redistribution-Mr. MacNicol
us. There was the difference in the size of the counties, the desire to retain county boundaries and the desire to create as little disturbance as possible. I ask them to believe that we have accomplished as good, as fair, as reasonable and as equitable a redistribution as has ever been accomplished in the history of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make a correction in the remarks of the hon. member for North Bruce. If I heard him correctly, he intimated that his new riding would have approximately 35,000 people.
I think I gave figures for three ridings, 32,900, 35,400 and 34,600.

If the riding of the member for North Bruce is carried out according to the bill it will contain a population of 29,842 while if it is carried out according to a proposal which was made, it will have a population of 27,789. I understood the hon. member to say 35,000.
I gave the figures for three ridings, and the 35,000 is for North Grey in which the city of Owen Sound is situated.

I should like to refer to
the remarks made by the hon. member with reference to South Toronto and I shall refer to city representations generally. While the committee was in session it was mentioned on many occasions that the two Brants should be put together. One of the reasons for this was that that county containing 53,000 odd contained the city of Brantford with a population of approximately 32,000. As a city member I know that the hon. member for Brantford City works very hard. A great deal of his time is taken up with correspondence in connection with the great industries located in that city. If my memory is correct, Brantford is the fourth largest manufacturing city in Canada. Having some fifty to sixty industries in my own riding I know full well what he must have to do to look after the requirements of the industries in his. A lot of people seem to think that a city member has nothing to do but my own experience is that I have to be here at nine o'clock in the morning and usually do not get away until twelve o'clock at night. If other city members work as I assume they do, they have lots to do.
The reason might be advanced that city voters do not vote. If my memory is correct, during the last elections approximately fifty per cent of the voters on the list in my riding voted. I represent a riding containing over 70,000 people. Many of these people
*say, "What is the use of going to the polls? The Conservative candidate will be elected anyway, and he does not need my vote." That is one of the reasons why the vote is frequently small in the cities. However, on the whole Canada stands up well with any nation in the world in the percentage of voters who vote. Something was said a moment ago about compulsory voting. I am opposed to compulsory voting and if it is ever brought up in the house I shall be prepared to advance many facts as arguments against such a method being adopted in this country. In the last general elections eighty-six per cent of the voters in North York voted. The percentage in the riding of Stormont was eighty-seven; in Kings eighty-nine. I see the hon. member for West Middlesex is checking these figures very carefully and I shall have to be careful because he agreed that if any constituency in Canada voted ninety per cent he would buy me a dinner. At this stage I think my
hon. friend will admit that he is too high in his percentages.

The percentage for Laval-Two Mountains was ninety and for Laprairie-Napierville, ninty-one. The percentage for the whole of Canada for the elections of 1930 was 76.1; for the elections of 1926. 70.1; for 1925, 68.7, and for 1921, 70.3. They have compulsory voting in Australia, the voters being fined when they do not vote. In the last general elections in that conutry, the vote ranged from ninety-one to ninety-four per cent. I think the people of Canada deserve a great deal of credit for the interest they take in elections and for the way they turn out to register their votes.

mittee on Ontario, and as a member of that committee I have a right to defend myself against any unjust attacks. The Minister of Public Works told us a few moments ago that redistribution creates disturbances in the constituencies, and that if it is left alone long enough people will settle down and will not be disturbed if they do not have a redistribution. Mr. Chairman, in discussing the present bill before the house, I wish it to be well understood that I am not championing my own personal interests, which have no place in this debate, but I do ask that fairness be shown to those who did me an honour in choosing me to represent them in the house. The measure under discussion provides for the annexation of the county of LTslet to that of Montmagny with the exception of the parishes of St. Roch, Ste. Louise, St. Damase, Tourville and Ste. Perpetue of the old county of L'Islet, and the parishes of St. Francois and Berthier of the old county of Montmagny.
The counties of LTslet and Montmagny were created in 1860, and their respective boundaries have always remained the same heretofore. I cannot see why it is necessary to carry out this change in 1933. This difference in population of 213 does not justify this change. LTslet, in 1923, was thought sufficiently populated, and after an increase of 1,545 within the last ten years, it is found too small and sacrificed to create an English speaking constituency in the city of Montreal.
The county of Montmagny with a population of 20,239 is considered too small and it is sacrificed to form a new county which will be known as Ohapleau, comprising a population of only 21,705 souls.	.
If we consider that the normal population of Montmagny is 22,000-that is according to the census of 1921-it is an outrage to suppress this county and create another having the same population and size. The reason given is that the city of Montreal has greatly increased and that, in the general interest, the counties of LTslet and Montmagny must be annexed.

Redistribution-Mr. Fafard
I greatly regret this decision; I should have preferred to see these old counties maintain their identity. However, if the general interest demands it, I accept the union, on condition that they be entirely merged and not cut up as the bill before the house intends to do.
Moreover, there is no reason to transfer parishes from one county or the other. The two counties united together form a population of 39,643, which is many thousands less than the unit fixed by the census of 1931. Besides, 50 per cent of the counties have a population of more than 40,000. If the wedding of these two counties is thought necessary in the interest of the country, as a whole, let us celebrate it in an atmosphere of peace, friendship and harmony, so that the union may have beneficial results to the people of the two counties united. Preserving their closely bound parochial, provincial and judicial institutions, they will live together in an atmosphere of peace, harmony and prosperity. Louise, St. Damase, Tourville and St. Perpetue, you place in the county of Kamouraska parishes which belonged to the judiciary district of Montmagny, and the parish of St. Pamphile will be so situated that the people of that parish will be unable to reach their principal town or the St. Lawrence river without passing through Kamouraska county.

There is another reason which might bespeak in favour of the complete annexation of the two counties. As the hon. member for Montmagny is well aware, farmers who are members of the society of agriculture, gather, at various seasons, at parish exhibitions. What will happen? A large number of the people of the old parishes of the county of L'Islet will no further be able to meet their friends. They will no doubt meet people as honest and friendly, however, a certain aloofness will exist in discussing farming questions.
As I stated at the outset of my remarks, the reasons which prompt me to protest against this bill are on a much higher plane than the political and personal interests of the two members. I am convinced-that is, I was-that the feelings that move me will be shared by the hon. member for Montmagny, known for his impartiality and broad-mindedness, and especially looked upon as the champion of minorities. I am convinced that after listening to the reasons given, he will wish for an intact Montmagny united to an intact L'Islet.
Mr. LaVERGNE (Translation): I have no objection.

I feel confident that after thinking it over he will recall that in the parishes, for instance, of St-Fran-gois and Berthier, at the last election, a minority of 255 conservatives voted and placed their trust in him. They were the ones who elected him in Montmagny, because his majority was 222 votes.
I shall even go further: in 1904, the hon. member for Montmagny was a highly gifted young man, with great resources, he came forward in politics bearing the standard of Laurier. The liberals of Berthier and St. Frangois cast their votes in his favour. He polled both the conservative and liberal votes in these two parishes, and I now wonder

whether, after thinking it over, the hon. member will cast aside the weapon that these people gave him in 1904, which permitted him to pass many years in political life, and which again they gave him in 1930, or whether he will now turn it against them.
Political life has a certain attraction; however, I would rather withdraw from it than be false to my people.
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Hear! hear!

All of us
were elected by people who trusted us. Let us not betray them whatever may be our political standard. AVe were sent here to represent our counties and not to cut them up. Let us be just, if we wish that justice be done to us. If the government persists in its policy, the public will soon note that the conservatives are panic stricken because, it is an extraordinary thing, the members opposite hardly wish to have anything to do with their constituencies this year; they would like to remove all those who heard them deliver speeches or make election promises.
This discussion, sir, cannot last very long, let us remember that when this Parliament is dissolved, the two present members of the counties of Montmagny and L'lslet, will equally disappear. Unless chosen by the convention, they cannot be candidates. Let us suppose that the hon. member for Montmagny is chosen by the convention-and I most heartily wish that he will be so favoured-I am certain that he would be more at ease, if he were able to state, from the hustings, that he championed the cause of minorities against a hostile majority. If my hon. friend, for personal reasons, decided to quit the political arena, he would equally be more satisfied in quitting the arena where he shone, thinking that he was true to the county that had placed their trust in him and that he had proved himself the champion of minorities.

House of Commons, Ottawa.
M.v dear colleague,
After seriously considering the question of redistribution of the constituencies in the province of Quebec, I have come to the conclusion that it would be preferable to follow the system adopted during the last forty years and to carry out the least changes possible in the rearrangement of counties. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as Wednesday is a statutory holiday-Victoria day, as it is described in the revised statutes-and Thursday is Ascension day, which to a number of hon. members is a day of obligation, I suggest, if it is acceptable to the house, that the house meet at three o'clock on Wednesday and on Thursday. That will enable those who have Arbor day duties and matters of that kind on hand for Wednesday to dispose of them, and I believe it is satisfactory to our friends if they have the morning free until three o'clock on Thursday. If that is acceptable I shall be glad to make arrangements accordingly, and would give notice that I shall move to-morrow morning in that sense.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
Tuesday, May 23, 1933
